docs.title: 1.1 Term and overnight indices
docs.text: An IborIndex (EURIBOR 1M–12M) fixes fixing_days business days before its value date and accrues to a maturity found by adding its tenor with modified following and the end-of-month rule. EURIBOR 3M fixed on Monday 15 January 2024 has value date 17 January and maturity 17 April 2024. An OvernightIndex (SOFR on the US-SIFMA calendar, €STR on TARGET, SONIA on the UK calendar) fixes every business day for the period up to the next business day. Published rates are stored by fixing date in a FixingHistory.

docs.title: 1.2 Compounding in arrears
docs.text:
For a period \([t_s, t_e)\) whose index business days are \(d_0 < \dots < d_{N-1}\), the compounded rate is

\[ R = \frac{1}{\tau}\Bigl[\prod_{i=0}^{N-1}\bigl(1 + r_i\,\tau_i\bigr) - 1\Bigr], \qquad \tau = \sum_i \tau_i, \]

where \(\tau_i\) is the index day-count fraction of the days on which \(r_i\) applies; the averaged rate is \(\sum_i r_i\tau_i/\tau\). A rate set on a Friday or before a holiday applies over the following non-business days. Over the SOFR week from 1 to 8 July 2024 (4 July is a US holiday) the fixings of 1, 2, 3 and 5 July carry weights \(1, 1, 2, 3\) over 360.

ISDA (2021) defines three ways of knowing the rate before payment. With a lookback of \(p\) days, each rate is the fixing \(p\) business days earlier while the weights stay those of the calculation period. With an observation shift, the whole observation period moves back \(p\) days and both rates and weights come from it. With a lockout of \(s\) days, the fixing of the lockout date, \(s\) business days before the period end, applies to the rest of the period. For the ISDA example period from 22 September to 22 December 2020 with \(s = 5\), the lockout date is 15 December and its rate applies from 15 to 21 December. A payment delay only moves the payment date.

docs.title: 1.3 Projection from a curve
docs.text:
The forward rate for the fixing on \(d_i\) is \(F_i = \bigl(P(d_i)/P(d_{i+1}) - 1\bigr)/\tau_i\). Without lookback, shift or lockout, the projected daily factors telescope:

\[ \prod_{i \ge j}(1 + F_i\tau_i) = \frac{P(d_j)}{P(t_e)}, \]

so projected_overnight_rate needs two discount factors beyond the last published fixing. The tests check that the shortcut equals the daily product to rounding.

docs.title: 2. Cashflows, legs and pricing
docs.text:
A leg is a list of coupons, each with a payment date and an amount(projection, fixings). A FixedCoupon pays \(N K \tau\), an IborCoupon pays \(N(\text{gearing}\cdot L + s)\tau\) with the term rate \(L\) fixed in advance, and an OvernightCoupon pays \(N R\tau\) with \(R\) compounded or averaged in arrears. fixed_leg, ibor_leg and overnight_leg build legs from a Schedule, with payment lags and notionals that may change period by period. The present value and the annuity are

\[ \mathrm{PV} = \sum_i \text{amount}_i\,P_d(t^{\text{pay}}_i), \qquad A = \sum_i N_i\tau_i\,P_d(t^{\text{pay}}_i), \]

summed over the coupons paid after the valuation date, with \(P_d\) the discount curve. Projected IBOR coupons use the index's own value and maturity dates. These can differ from the coupon dates when a start date has been rolled. With use_index_dates=False they use the coupon dates instead, and on a single curve a floating leg then telescopes exactly to \(N\bigl(P(t_0) - P(t_n)\bigr)\) when there is no payment lag.

docs.title: 3.1 Deposits and FRAs
docs.text:
A deposit starting at spot pays \(N(1 + R\tau)\) at maturity. A forward rate agreement on \([t_s, t_e]\) settles at \(t_s\) the discounted difference between the fixing and the contract rate, so its value is

\[ \mathrm{PV}_{\text{FRA}} = N\,\frac{\tau(F - K)}{1 + \tau F}\,P_d(t_s), \qquad F = \frac{1}{\tau}\Bigl(\frac{P_p(t_s)}{P_p(t_e)} - 1\Bigr). \]

A 3×6 EURIBOR FRA traded on 15 January 2024 accrues from 17 April to 17 July 2024.

docs.title: 3.2 Term-rate futures
docs.text:
Daily margining makes the futures rate the risk-neutral expectation of the fixing, which exceeds the forward. In the Hull–White model \(dr = (\vartheta(t) - ar)\,dt + \sigma\,dW\), with \(B(t) = (1 - e^{-at})/a\) and \(B_{ij} = B(t_j - t_i)\),

\[ 1 + \tau R^{\text{fut}} = (1 + \tau F)\,e^{\Gamma}, \qquad \Gamma = \sigma^2 B_{12}\Bigl[B_{12}\,\frac{1 - e^{-2at_1}}{2a} + \tfrac12 B_{01}^2\Bigr]. \]

As \(a \to 0\) (Ho–Lee), \(\Gamma \to \sigma^2\tau t_1(t_1 + 2\tau)/2\). For \(\sigma = 1\%\), \(t_1 = 1\) and \(\tau = 0.25\), this gives \(\Gamma = 1.875 \times 10^{-5}\). IMM dates are the third Wednesdays of March, June, September and December; imm_code and imm_from_code translate them to contract codes such as H24.

docs.title: 3.3 SOFR futures
docs.text:
A three-month SOFR future settles on the rate compounded over its IMM quarter. The March 2024 contract runs from 20 March to 19 June 2024, an accrual of \(91/360\). The one-month contract settles on the arithmetic average over a calendar month. Write each daily factor as \(1 + r_i\tau_i = 1/P(t_i, t_{i+1})\). Under the \(t_N\)-forward measure the product telescopes, so its expectation is \(1 + \tau F = P(0, t_0)/P(0, t_N)\). In a Gaussian model \(Y = \log\prod_i 1/P(t_i, t_{i+1})\) is Gaussian, and changing to the risk-neutral measure multiplies the expectation by \(e^{\mathrm{Cov}(Y, \int_0^{t_N} r)}\). In Hull–White this gives, exactly for the daily product,

\[ 1 + \tau R^{\text{fut}} = (1 + \tau F)\,e^{\Gamma_c}, \qquad \Gamma_c = \sum_{t_i > 0} B(t_{i+1} - t_i)\,c(t_i; t_N), \qquad c(t; T) = \sigma^2\Bigl[\tfrac12 B(t)^2 + B(T - t)\,\frac{1 - e^{-2at}}{2a}\Bigr], \]

where \(c(t; T) = \mathrm{Cov}\bigl(x(t), \int_0^T x\bigr)\) for the Gaussian factor \(x\). Fixings already published do not contribute. The continuous limit is \(\Gamma_c = \mathrm{Var}(I) + \mathrm{Cov}\bigl(\int_0^{T_s} r, I\bigr)\) with \(I = \int_{T_s}^{T_e} r\), which for Ho–Lee is

\[ \Gamma_c = \sigma^2\bigl(\tau^2 T_s + \tau^3/3 + \tau T_s^2/2\bigr). \]

For \(\sigma = 1\%\), \(T_s = 1\) and \(\tau = 0.25\), this gives \(\Gamma_c = 1.927083 \times 10^{-5}\), more than the term-rate \(\Gamma\) because the rate is still being fixed during the quarter. For the same reason a spot-starting quarter keeps \(\sigma^2\tau^3/3 = 5.208 \times 10^{-7}\). The tests check \(c\) against the Itô-isometry integral, the Ho–Lee formula, and an exact G1++ Monte Carlo of both contract types.

docs.title: 4.1 Par rates and identities
docs.text:
A Swap exchanges a fixed leg for a floating leg. For the payer of fixed,

\[ \mathrm{PV} = \mathrm{PV}_{\text{float}} - \mathrm{PV}_{\text{fixed}} = (S - K)\,A, \qquad S = \frac{\mathrm{PV}_{\text{float}}}{A}, \]

and on a single curve without payment lags \(S = N\bigl(P(t_s) - P(t_e)\bigr)/A\). The par spread is the margin over the floating index that makes the swap worth zero.

ois_swap builds overnight-indexed swaps: both legs follow one annual schedule on the index calendar, the floating leg compounds in arrears, and payments lag by two business days. A 5-year SOFR OIS traded on Monday 15 January 2024 (Martin Luther King Day) starts on 18 January 2024. Its first payment is on 23 January 2025 and its last on 22 January 2029. vanilla_swap builds fixed-versus-IBOR swaps with the EUR conventions (annual 30/360 against the index tenor). A 10-year swap against EURIBOR 6M traded on 15 January 2024 starts on 17 January and has 10 fixed and 20 floating periods. Its second fixed period ends on the rolled date 19 January 2026, so it accrues \(362/360\). basis_swap exchanges two floating legs, for example EURIBOR 3M plus a spread against EURIBOR 6M. On a single curve, with coupon-date projection, its par spread is zero to \(10^{-14}\).

docs.title: 4.2 Risk measures
docs.text:
pv01 is the change in value for a one basis point rise in the fixed rate, \(10^{-4}A\). dv01 is the central difference of the value when both curves are shifted by one basis point in continuously compounded zero rate. For an OIS on a flat curve the tests compare it with the analytic derivative

\[ \mathrm{DV01} = 10^{-4}\Bigl[N\bigl(-t_s P(t_s) + t_e P(t_e)\bigr) + K\sum_i N\tau_i\,t_i\,P(t_i)\Bigr] \]

to \(10^{-6}\). For an at-the-money swap, DV01 and PV01 agree within a few percent.

docs.title: 4.3 Amortising and accreting swaps
docs.text: The notional may be a sequence (one entry per period) or a function of the accrual start date, such as step_notional or linear_notional. Each coupon is linear in its notional. A swap whose notional steps down by \(\Delta N_j\) at \(T_j\) is therefore exactly the sum of bullet swaps of notional \(\Delta N_j\) maturing at \(T_j\), and its par rate is the annuity-weighted average of their par rates. The tests verify this for OIS and vanilla swaps, including their DV01.

docs.title: 5. Fixed-rate bonds
docs.text:
FixedRateBond generates an unadjusted coupon schedule with payments rolled to the following business day. Accrued interest uses the reference periods that ACT/ACT ICMA requires. With \(n\) coupons a year, settlement \(t_s\), next coupon \(t_1\) and \(w = n\,\tau_{\text{ICMA}}(t_s, t_1)\), the street-convention dirty price at yield \(y\) is

\[ P_{\text{dirty}} = \sum_{j \ge 1} \frac{c_j}{(1 + y/n)^{w + j - 1}}, \]

and the clean price is the dirty price minus accrued interest. Macaulay duration is the time-weighted average of the discounted cash flows. Modified duration divides it by \(1 + y/n\), and convexity is the second derivative of the price divided by the price. dirty_price_from_curve discounts on a curve with an optional z-spread added to continuously compounded zero rates, and z_spread inverts it.

For a 10-year 5% semi-annual bond issued on 15 January 2024 and valued on that date:

Quantity Value Dirty price at a 6% yield 92.56126256977227 Clean price at a 5% yield 100 Macaulay duration at 5% 7.98945 years Accrued interest on 15 March 2024 \(2.5 \times 60/182 = 0.824176\) Clean price at 5% on 15 March 2024 99.99319

The 2034 final coupon falls on Sunday 15 January and Monday 16 January is Martin Luther King Day, so it is paid on 17 January 2034. The accrual still ends on the unadjusted date.

docs.title: 6.1 Piecewise curves
docs.text:
A PiecewiseCurve stores discount factors \(P_i\) at node times \(t_i\), with the node \((0, 1)\) prepended. An interpolation scheme turns them into a smooth \(x(t) = -\log P(t)\), and the instantaneous forward \(f = x'\) is the scheme's analytic derivative. Following Hagan & West (Interpolation methods for curve construction, 2006), the schemes are:

Scheme Interpolates Forward Local LogLinearDiscount \(\log P\) linearly piecewise flat yes LinearZero zero rate \(r\) linearly piecewise linear in \(t\), jumps at nodes yes CubicZero \(r\) by a cubic spline \(C^1\) no CubicSplineRT \(rt\) by a cubic spline \(C^1\) no MonotoneCubicRT \(rt\) by Hyman-filtered Hermite cubics \(C^0\) nearly MonotoneConvex discrete forwards, Hagan–West monotone convex \(C^0\); positive with positivity=True when the discrete forwards are nearly

Monotone convex reproduces each discrete forward \(f^d_i = (x_i - x_{i-1})/(t_i - t_{i-1})\) as the average of \(f\) over its interval. With zero rates 2.75%, 4%, 4.75%, 5%, 4.75% at 1–5 years, it gives forwards 0.0229375, 0.05010625, 0.0609 and 0.03625 at 0.3, 1.3, 2.1 and 4.5 years.

compare_schemes scores schemes on Hagan and West's criteria: minimum forward, roughness \(\int f'^2\), locality, and the largest forward move per unit zero-rate bump. On the hump-and-dip curve with zero rates 8.1%, 7%, 4.4%, 7%, 4%, 3% at 0.1, 1, 4, 9, 20 and 30 years:

  • LinearZero and CubicZero produce negative forwards, while MonotoneConvex stays positive.
  • LogLinearDiscount has minimum forward \((0.03 \cdot 30 - 0.04 \cdot 20)/10 = 0.01\).
  • A bump to \(r_j\) moves the log-linear flat forward on \((t_{j-1}, t_j)\) by \(t_j/(t_j - t_{j-1})\) per unit, and on \((t_j, t_{j+1})\) by \(-t_j/(t_{j+1} - t_j)\). Its largest sensitivity is therefore \(30/10 = 3\), reached at the last node.
  • The natural splines spread a single bump across the curve. One bump can move the CubicSplineRT forward on all six intervals and the CubicZero forward on five, against at most two for the monotone schemes.

docs.title: 6.2 Helpers and the bootstrap
docs.text:
A helper is a quoted instrument that can compute its model quote on a mapping of named curves. Its pillar is the last date the quote depends on. bootstrap_curve sorts the helpers by pillar and puts a node at each pillar. It then solves node \(i\), in \(x_i = -\log P(t_i)\) with Brent's method, so that helper \(i\) reprices. Projection curves are built on a known discount curve (dual-curve bootstrapping) by passing known={"discount": ois}.

The two kinds of scheme behave differently:

  • Local schemes. Later nodes do not move the curve before \(t_i\), so one pass reprices every helper to rounding.
  • Non-local schemes. The passes repeat until the nodes stop moving.

fit_curves instead solves every node of several curves at once by Newton's method, with a finite-difference Jacobian. This handles cases a sequential bootstrap cannot: for example, long ESTR points that exist only through ESTR/EURIBOR basis swaps, which need both curves at once. For a single curve it converges to the same nodes.

BootstrapResult.jacobian returns \(J_{ij} = \partial q_i/\partial x_j\) at the solution. It is lower triangular for a local scheme. By the implicit function theorem, node_sensitivities returns \(\partial x/\partial q = J^{-1}\): the move of each node per unit move of one quote with the others fixed, which is exactly the re-bootstrapped curve.

docs.title: 6.3 Front end, futures and turns
docs.text:
Deposit.overnight, Deposit.tom_next and Deposit.spot_next pin the curve between the trade date and spot. Traded on Friday 8 March 2024, the O/N deposit runs over the weekend to Monday, an accrual of \(3/360\). With O/N and T/N helpers, \(P(t_{\text{spot}}) = 1/\bigl((1 + \tau_{ON} r_{ON})(1 + \tau_{TN} r_{TN})\bigr)\).

quarterly_futures builds a strip of consecutive 3M overnight futures from the next IMM date. Each FutureHelper carries Hull–White parameters \((a, \sigma)\) for the convexity adjustment of §3.3. With the right parameters, the strip recovers the forwards of the curve that produced the prices. With zero convexity the curve forward \(F'\) equals the futures rate. It therefore overstates the true forward \(F\) by exactly \(1 + \tau F' = (1 + \tau F)e^{\Gamma_c}\).

Year-end funding pressure lifts the overnight forward over the turn. turn_of_year(year, s) returns a ForwardSpread adding \(s\) to the instantaneous forward from the last business day of the year to the first of the next: from 31 December 2024 to 2 January 2025, or, with the 2022 year end on a Saturday, from 30 December 2022 to 2 January 2023. A SpreadAdjustedCurve multiplies the base discount factor by \(e^{-s\,|[t_a, t_b) \cap [0, t)|}\). With spreads= passed to bootstrap_curve, the smooth base curve is fitted under the known turn.

docs.title: 6.4 Policy-meeting curves
docs.text: Overnight rates step on central-bank meeting dates. flat_forward_curve holds the forward at \(r_j\) on \([s_{j-1}, s_j)\), which is LogLinearDiscount with nodes at the step dates. meeting_date_curve fits one rate per inter-meeting period to any helpers. The fit is exact with one helper per period, and Gauss–Newton least squares when there are more, for example monthly SOFR futures, several of which can fall between two FOMC meetings. A period that no helper depends on makes the Jacobian rank-deficient, and the fit raises ValueError rather than invent a rate.

docs.title: 6.5 Parametric curves
docs.text:
Svensson's curve, with \(x_k = t/\tau_k\) and \(L(x) = (1 - e^{-x})/x\), has

\[ z(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 L(x_1) + \beta_2\bigl(L(x_1) - e^{-x_1}\bigr) + \beta_3\bigl(L(x_2) - e^{-x_2}\bigr), \qquad f(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 e^{-x_1} + \beta_2 x_1 e^{-x_1} + \beta_3 x_2 e^{-x_2}, \]

so \(f(0) = z(0^+) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\) and \(z(\infty) = \beta_0\). Nelson–Siegel is \(\beta_3 = 0\). The model is linear in the betas for fixed decay times, so fit_nss_zero_rates uses variable projection: a search over \(\log\tau\) with a linear least-squares solve inside. fit_nss fits helper quotes, bonds included, by Levenberg–Marquardt.

docs.title: 6.6 Curve sets
docs.text: A CurveSet is a mapping of named curves with a discount role and an index-to-curve projection map. Helpers read it directly, and pv prices swaps and basis swaps by the index on each floating leg.

docs.title: 7.1 Node and quote deltas
docs.text:
A fitted curve is a function of its node values \(x_j = -\log P(t_j)\), and a price \(V\) is a function of the curves. node_deltas returns \(\partial V/\partial x_j\) by central differences, leaving the interpolation scheme and any turn spreads in place. The fit makes the helper model quotes \(m(x)\) equal to the market quotes \(q\). By the implicit function theorem \(\partial x/\partial q = J^{-1}\) with \(J = \partial m/\partial x\), so

\[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial q} = J^{-\top}\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}. \]

quote_deltas evaluates this from one Jacobian instead of one re-bootstrap per quote. The result is the sensitivity to each quote with the others held fixed, exactly what bumping a quote and refitting gives. It takes a single-curve BootstrapResult or a multi-curve GlobalFitResult. For the latter, nodes and helpers are stacked across curves, so cross effects are included.

A par swap identical to helper \(i\) is a useful check. Its value is \((S - K)A\), and with the other quotes fixed only its own par rate \(S = q_i\) can move. Its quote deltas are therefore exactly \(A\,e_i\): the annuity on its own quote and zero elsewhere, OIS quotes included in a dual-curve fit.

docs.title: 7.2 Key-rate deltas
docs.text:
Key-rate deltas (Ho, 1992) need no fit. The zero curve of any YieldCurve is moved by triangular hats \(h_k(t)\) centred on key tenors and flat beyond the first and last keys:

\[ P'(t) = P(t)\exp\Bigl(-t\sum_k b_k\,h_k(t)\Bigr). \]

The hats sum to one, so key-rate deltas add up to the parallel delta to first order. A zero-coupon bond maturing on a key has delta \(-T\,P(T)\) on that key and none elsewhere. At a flat 3% continuously compounded rate, this is \(-5e^{-0.15} = -4.30354\) for \(T = 5\).

docs.title: 7.3 Hedging and P&L explain
docs.text:
hedge_notionals minimises \(\lVert W^{1/2}(d + Hn)\rVert_2\) over hedge notionals \(n\), where \(d\) is the book's risk and column \(j\) of \(H\) is the risk of one unit of hedge \(j\). With par swaps on every pillar, \(H\) is diagonal with the annuities, so \(n_i = -d_i/A_i\). With fewer hedges than buckets, the residual is \(W\)-orthogonal to every hedge.

Between two fits on the same nodes, pnl_explain splits the change in value into \(\delta^\top\Delta x\) and \(\tfrac12\Delta x^\top\Gamma\Delta x\), with \(\Gamma\) from node_gamma. The remainder is third order. For a zero-coupon bond on a node it is exactly \(-P\,\Delta x^3/6\) to leading order. For an 8-year OIS, multiplying a market move by five multiplies the remainder by about \(5^3 = 125\).

docs.title: 7.4 Principal components
docs.text: curve_pca diagonalises the sample covariance of zero-rate changes on fixed tenors. Its first three loadings are level, slope and curvature (Litterman & Scheinkman, 1991). Signs are fixed so that the level loadings sum to a positive number, the slope rises from short to long tenors, and the curvature is positive at the middle tenor. For a book with key-rate deltas \(d\) on the same tenors, the factor deltas are \(d^\top v_j\). The book's P&L variance under the retained factors is \(\sum_j\lambda_j(d^\top v_j)^2\), which equals the first-order P&L variance when the changes have exactly that rank.

docs.title: 8.1 Caps, floors and swaptions
docs.text:
A caplet on a term index fixing at \(T\) for the period \([t_s, t_e]\) pays \(\tau(L - K)^+\) at \(t_e\). Under the \(t_e\)-forward measure \(L\) is a martingale, so its value is \(P(t_e)\,\tau\,\mathrm{Black}(F, K, T, \sigma)\), with \(F\) the forward from the projection curve and \(P\) from the discount curve. CapFloor.price accepts Black, shifted Black or normal (Bachelier) vols, either one flat number or a function \(\sigma(T, K)\). cap_floor skips the first period by default, since it is already fixed: a 5Y EURIBOR6M cap has 9 caplets. Caps minus floors at the same strike equal the floating leg minus \(K\) times the caplet annuity.

A physically settled payer swaption is a call on the forward swap rate \(S\) under the annuity measure, worth \(A\,\mathrm{Black}(S, K, T, \sigma)\). Cash-settled swaptions use the cash annuity

\[ \bar A(S) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1/m}{(1 + S/m)^i} = \frac{1 - (1 + S/m)^{-n}}{S}, \]

which cash_annuity evaluates without cancellation as \(S \to 0\).

docs.title: 8.2 SABR
docs.text: In SABR (Hagan et al., 2002) \(dF = \alpha F^ eta dW\) and \(d\alpha = u\alpha\,dZ\), with \(d\langle W, Z angle = ho\,dt\). SABR.lognormal_vol gives Hagan's expansion, or Obłój's (2008) correction with method="obloj". The two agree at the money. They differ in the wings even at \(T = 0\): with \(\alpha = 0.035\), \( eta = 0.5\), \( ho = -0.3\), \( u = 0.4\) and \(F = 0.03\), at \(K = F/e\) Hagan gives \(0.35902\) and Obłój \(0.36024\). calibrate_sabr fixes \( eta\) and fits \((\alpha, ho, u)\) to a smile by least squares. If an ATM vol is given, it solves for \(\alpha\) from that vol through alpha_from_atm, so the ATM quote is matched exactly. A shift \(s\) applies the model to \(F + s\), for negative rates.

docs.title: 8.3 Arbitrage-free SABR
docs.text:
At long expiries and low rates, Hagan's formula implies a negative density near zero. ArbitrageFreeSABR instead solves the effective one-dimensional forward equation of Hagan et al. (2014) for the density, with absorbing mass at the boundary, using the variable \(z\) and the Lawson–Swayne scheme of Le Floc'h & Kennedy (2017):

\[ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 (M Q)}{\partial F^2}, \qquad M = \tfrac12 D(F)^2 E(F, T). \]

Mass and the forward are conserved to rounding error. For \(\alpha = 0.02\), \(\beta = 0.5\), \(\rho = -0.3\), \(\nu = 0.5\), \(F = 1\%\) and \(T = 10\), Hagan's prices have a negative density near zero, while the PDE puts \(8.74\%\) of the mass at zero. With \(\beta = 0\) and \(\nu = 0\) the model is Brownian motion absorbed at zero, and the PDE converges to the reflection-principle prices at second order.

sabr_paths simulates the model itself, with absorption at zero. With \(\beta = 0\) it adds a Brownian-bridge crossing test, which removes the \(O(\sqrt{\Delta t})\) bias of checking only at the grid times. The PDE is an expansion of the true dynamics, so at long expiries its prices differ from Monte Carlo by more than sampling error.

docs.title: 8.4 Caplet stripping and the swaption cube
docs.text:
Cap markets quote one flat vol per maturity. strip_caplet_vols turns these into caplet vols by bootstrapping. It sorts the caps by maturity and gives the caplets that each longer cap adds one common vol, chosen so that the cap reprices; earlier caplets keep the vols already stripped. The result is a piecewise-constant CapletVolCurve in expiry, usable directly as \(\sigma(T, K)\) in CapFloor.price. If flat vols fall faster than the bootstrap can absorb, the required caplet variance becomes negative and the function raises.

SwaptionCube holds one SABR smile per (expiry, tenor) node, with a common \(\beta\). Between nodes it interpolates \(\log\alpha\), \(\rho\) and \(\log\nu\) bilinearly, which keeps \(\alpha, \nu > 0\) and \(|\rho| < 1\). Beyond the matrix the parameters are held flat.

docs.title: 8.5 CMS
docs.text:
A coupon paying the swap rate \(S_T\) at \(T_p\) is worth \(A_0\,E^A[S_T\,\alpha(S_T)]\), where the annuity mapping \(\alpha(S) \approx P(T, T_p)/A(T)\) comes from a terminal swap-rate model. CMSReplication evaluates such expectations by Carr–Madan replication with swaption prices:

\[ E^A[f(S_T)] = f(S_0) + \int_{-\infty}^{S_0} f''(K)\,P(K)\,dK + \int_{S_0}^{\infty} f''(K)\,C(K)\,dK. \]

The standard mapping (Hagan, 2003) is \(\alpha \propto G(S) = S(1 + S/m)^{-\delta}/(1 - (1 + S/m)^{-n})\). The linear mapping is \(\alpha(S) = P(T_p)/A_0 + a(S - S_0)\). With the linear mapping and a lognormal swap rate, the convexity adjustment has the closed form

\[ E^{T_p}[S_T] - S_0 = \frac{a A_0}{P(T_p)}\,S_0^2\,\bigl(e^{\sigma^2 T} - 1\bigr), \]

which the replication reproduces to \(10^{-8}\) relative. With the slope \(a\) taken from the standard mapping, the adjustment for a 5-year fixing of a 10-year annual swap rate at \(S_0 = 3\%\) and \(\sigma = 20\%\) is \(10.2\) bp. The standard mapping itself gives \(10.8\) bp. The smile matters as well. The payoff is most convex at high rates, so raising the vols at high strikes (a larger \(\nu\)) raises the adjustment, while a downward skew (\(\beta < 1\), \(\rho < 0\)) lowers it; examples/rates_vol_example.py shows the second case.

docs.title: 9.1 Hull–White
docs.text:
HullWhite writes the short rate as \(r_t = f(0, t) + x_t\) with

\[ dx_t = \bigl(y(t) - a x_t\bigr)\,dt + \sigma(t)\,dW_t, \qquad x_0 = 0, \qquad y(t) = \int_0^t e^{-2a(t-u)}\sigma(u)^2\,du, \]

which fits the discount curve by construction (Andersen & Piterbarg's form; \(\sigma\) may be piecewise constant). Bond prices are \(P(t, T) = \frac{P(0,T)}{P(0,t)}\exp\bigl(-B x_t - \tfrac12 B^2 y(t)\bigr)\) with \(B = (1 - e^{-a(T-t)})/a\), so zero-bond options are Black formulas on the bond forward, and caplets are bond puts. A swap with discount-curve cashflows (swap_cashflows, with the projection basis kept as a deterministic spread) is a portfolio of bonds. When its amounts change sign once, Jamshidian's decomposition prices the swaption as bond options struck at \(P(T, t_i | x^*)\). Otherwise swaption integrates against the Gaussian.

docs.title: 9.2 Trees, PDE and simulation
docs.text: HullWhiteTree is the Hull–White (1994) trinomial tree, with the drift fitted step by step so that every grid bond reprices exactly. HullWhitePDE solves the pricing equation in \(x\) on the spxa.pde solvers, with exercise events and American constraints. hull_white_paths simulates \((x, \int x)\) exactly, so the bank-account discount factor reprices the curve without bias. These engines handle early exercise. On a flat 3% curve, with \(a = 0.05\) and \(\sigma = 1\%\), an American put expiring in 2 years on the 6-year bond, struck at \(P(0, 6)\), is worth \(0.0094954\), against \(0.0020894\) for the European. Exercise pays as soon as rates fall far enough to lift the bond above its current price.

docs.title: 9.3 Calibration
docs.text: calibrate_hull_white fixes \(a\) and fits \(\sigma\) to swaptions or caps. In bootstrap mode, \(\sigma\) is piecewise constant between instrument expiries and each level is solved in turn. In global mode, \(a\) and one \(\sigma\) are fitted together by least squares. calibrate_g2pp fits all five G2++ parameters to a grid of swaptions. It keeps \(a > b\) (so \(x\) is the fast factor) and \(|\rho| < 1\) through its parametrisation, and it recovers the parameters of a synthetic \(3 \times 3\) grid to \(10^{-5}\). model_implied_vols quotes any ShortRateModel (Hull–White, G2++, CIR++) in Black or Bachelier vols for comparison with the market.

docs.title: 9.4 G2++ and the two-factor Hull–White model
docs.text: In G2++ (Brigo & Mercurio, §4.2) \(r = x + y + \varphi(t)\), with two correlated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck factors of speeds \(a, b\) and vols \(\sigma, \eta\). Bonds stay exponential-affine. Swaptions reduce to a one-dimensional integral: given \(x_T\), the payoff is monotone in \(y_T\), and the conditional expectation is a sum of normal distribution functions. Correlation decorrelates the curve: a negative \(\rho\) cancels part of the short-end variance while long rates follow the slow factor. With \(a = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1.2\%\), \(b = 0.05\) and \(\eta = 0.9\%\), a 5Y×20Y swaption is worth \(12.2\) times a 5Y×1Y at \(\rho = -0.7\), and \(8.3\) times at \(\rho = 0.7\). Hull and White's two-factor model, with a stochastic drift \(u\) in the short rate, is the same model: HullWhite2F.to_g2pp and from_g2pp map the parameters both ways, preserving the instantaneous covariance of \((dr, du)\).

docs.title: 9.5 Positive rates: Black–Karasinski and CIR++
docs.text: Gaussian models give negative rates. For \(a = 0.1\) and \(\sigma = 0.85\%\), the 10-year Hull–White tree reaches \(-9.2\%\) at its lowest node. In Black–Karasinski \(\log r\) is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, so rates stay positive. There are no closed forms, so BlackKarasinskiTree solves for each step's drift by Newton's method to fit the curve, and black_karasinski_paths simulates on the fitted drift. CIR++ (Brigo & Mercurio, 2001) shifts a CIR factor by \(\varphi = f^M - f^{\rm CIR}\). It keeps CIR's closed forms: bond options are scaled non-central \(\chi^2\) formulas, and swaptions follow by Jamshidian, since bond prices decrease in \(x\). Rates stay above \(\varphi\). With \(\kappa = 0.3\), \(\theta = 2.5\%\), \(\sigma = 0.08\) and \(x_0 = 2\%\) on the flat 3% curve, \(\varphi\) is positive out to 30 years. The square-root diffusion also produces a smile. For a 2Y×5Y swaption at the money and \(\pm 100\) bp, this CIR++ gives normal vols of \(27.48\), \(46.42\) and \(57.09\) bp, while Hull–White (\(a = 0.05\), \(\sigma = 1\%\)) is nearly flat at \(86.64\), \(87.14\) and \(87.65\) bp.

docs.title: 10.1 Gaussian HJM
docs.text:
Heath, Jarrow and Morton model the whole forward curve. With a deterministic vector volatility \(\sigma(t, T)\) driving independent Brownian motions,

\[ df(t, T) = \sigma(t, T)\cdot\Sigma(t, T)\,dt + \sigma(t, T)\cdot dW_t, \qquad \Sigma(t, T) = \int_t^T \sigma(t, s)\,ds, \]

and the drift is forced by no-arbitrage, so GaussianHJM fits the initial curve for any choice of volatility. Bonds are lognormal, and under the \(T\)-forward measure \(P(t, S)/P(t, T)\) has log-variance \(\int_0^T |\Sigma(u, S) - \Sigma(u, T)|^2\,du\). Bond options and caplets are therefore Black formulas. exponential_vol (\(\sigma e^{-a(T-t)}\)) gives Hull–White, and two exponential factors with correlated loadings give G2++. GaussianHJM.from_hull_white covers piecewise-constant volatility: its jump times are passed as breakpoints, so the quadrature never straddles a jump. hump_vol gives \((\alpha + \beta\tau)e^{-\gamma\tau}\) in time to maturity \(\tau = T - t\). It peaks at \(\tau = 1/\gamma - \alpha/\beta\), the hump seen in historical forward-rate volatilities.

docs.title: 10.2 Simulating the curve
docs.text: hjm_paths evolves log deflated bonds \(Z(t, T_j) = P(t, T_j)/B(t)\) on a maturity grid. Each step freezes \(\Sigma\) at its start, and the increment \(-\tfrac12|\Sigma|^2\Delta t - \Sigma\cdot\Delta W\) has \(E[e^{\cdot}] = 1\) exactly. Every \(Z(\cdot, T_j)\) is then a discrete martingale, and the curve is repriced with no discretisation bias. The deflator is \(Z(t, t)\). The remaining error sits in option prices, through the left-point variance \(\sum_k |\Sigma(t_k, S) - \Sigma(t_k, T)|^2\Delta t\). The simulated payoff is priced exactly by Black at that variance, which converges at first order.

docs.title: 10.3 Cheyette
docs.text:
A separable volatility \(\sigma_r(t)\,e^{-\kappa(T - t)}\) makes HJM Markovian in two states. Cheyette's model (Andersen & Piterbarg, ch. 13) lets the short-rate volatility depend on the state, \(\sigma_r(t, x)\), while keeping that structure:

\[ dx = (y - \kappa x)\,dt + \sigma_r\,dW, \qquad dy = (\sigma_r^2 - 2\kappa y)\,dt, \qquad P(t, T) = \frac{P(0, T)}{P(0, t)}e^{-G x - \frac12 G^2 y}, \]

with \(G = (1 - e^{-\kappa(T - t)})/\kappa\). Cheyette uses the linear local volatility \(\sigma_r = \max(\sigma(t) + \beta x, 0)\). With \(\beta = 0\), \(y\) is deterministic and the model is Hull–White. A positive \(\beta\) raises the volatility as rates rise, which produces the upward-sloping normal-vol skew of rate markets.

docs.title: 10.4 Engines
docs.text: cheyette_paths freezes \(\sigma_r\) and \(y\) over each step and solves the step exactly. For \(\beta = 0\) this is the exact Hull–White transition. CheyettePDE solves the two-dimensional pricing equation. Because \(y\) has no diffusion, each step splits into semi-Lagrangian advection in \(y\) and an implicit solve in \(x\) on each \(y\)-slice. Exercise dates apply \(\max(V, g)\), so the PDE prices American and Bermudan claims as well.

docs.title: 10.5 Swaptions and calibration
docs.text: cheyette_swaption follows Andersen & Piterbarg's projection. Freezing \(y\) at \(\bar y(t)\), the swap-rate volatility \(S_x\sigma_r\) is linearised into a displaced diffusion \(\lambda(t)(b(t)S + (1 - b(t))S_0)\). The skew is averaged with weights \(\lambda^2(t)\int_0^t\lambda^2\) (Piterbarg), and the swaption is priced in displaced Black. For a 2Y×5Y swaption with \(\kappa = 0.05\) and \(\sigma = 1\%\) on the flat 3% curve, the averaged skew is \(\bar b = 0.04\) at \(\beta = 0\) and \(1.21\) at \(\beta = 0.3\). With \(\beta = 0.3\) the PDE gives normal vols of \(70.6\), \(85.9\) and \(100.7\) bp at strikes \(2.5\%\), \(3.46\%\) and \(4.5\%\), and the approximation gives \(71.0\), \(86.5\) and \(101.5\) bp, within 1 bp across the smile. With \(\beta = 0\) the same strikes are nearly flat, at \(86.7\), \(87.1\) and \(87.6\) bp. calibrate_cheyette fits one \(\sigma\) level per expiry, plus \(\beta\), to a grid of strikes at each expiry using this formula.

docs.title: 11.1 Parametrisation
docs.text:
The LIBOR market model (Brace, Gątarek & Musiela; Jamshidian) takes the simply compounded forwards \(L_i\) on a tenor structure \(T_0 < \dots < T_n\) as its state. Each one is lognormal under its own payment measure, possibly displaced by \(\delta\):

\[ dL_i = \sigma_i(t)\,(L_i + \delta)\,dW_i^{T_{i+1}}, \qquad d\langle W_i, W_j\rangle = \rho_{ij}\,dt, \]

so caplets are Black formulas, exactly as quoted. LiborMarketModel uses Rebonato's time-homogeneous shape \(\sigma_i(t) = k_i f(T_i - t)\) with \(f(\tau) = (a + b\tau)e^{-c\tau} + d\) (AbcdVol). Its hump sits at \(\tau = 1/c - a/b\), which is \(1.72\) years for \((a, b, c, d) = (0.05, 0.09, 0.44, 0.11)\). AbcdVol.covariance integrates \(f(T_i - t)f(T_j - t)\) in closed form. The correlation is exponential_correlation, \(e^{-\beta|T_i - T_j|}\), or Rebonato's rebonato_correlation, \(\rho_\infty + (1 - \rho_\infty)e^{-\beta|T_i - T_j|}\). reduce_rank keeps its leading principal components and renormalises the diagonal. On 20 semi-annual forwards with \(\beta = 0.1\) and \(\rho_\infty = 0.4\), three factors leave a largest correlation error of \(0.089\).

docs.title: 11.2 Simulation
docs.text:
lmm_paths simulates the log displaced forwards under the spot LIBOR measure, whose numeraire rolls over the shortest bond. Forward \(i\) then has drift

\[ \sigma_i\sum_{j = q(t)}^{i}\frac{\tau_j\rho_{ij}\sigma_j(L_j + \delta)}{1 + \tau_j L_j}, \]

summed over the forwards still alive. Each step draws Gaussian increments with the exact integrated covariance of the step, so only the drift is discretised. It is either frozen at the start of the step or averaged with a predicted end value (predictor–corrector). The deflator \(P(0, T_0)/\prod_{j<k}(1 + \tau_j L_j(T_j))\) prices any payoff fixed on the tenor dates. Deflated bonds are martingales, and caplets reproduce Black within Monte Carlo error.

docs.title: 11.3 Swaptions and calibration
docs.text:
The forward swap rate over \([T_\alpha, T_\beta]\) is a weighted average \(S = \sum_i w_i L_i\), with \(w_i = \tau_i P(0, T_{i+1})/A\). Freezing the weights and the forwards gives Rebonato's formula (LiborMarketModel.swaption_vol):

\[ \sigma_{\alpha\beta}^2 T_\alpha = \frac{1}{(S + \delta)^2}\sum_{i, j = \alpha}^{\beta - 1} w_i w_j (L_i + \delta)(L_j + \delta)\,\rho_{ij}\int_0^{T_\alpha}\sigma_i\sigma_j\,dt. \]

The swaption is then Black on the annuity. On the flat 3% curve, the abcd shape above with the Rebonato correlation gives a 2Y×5Y volatility of \(17.84\%\), at an ATM swap rate of \(3.02\%\). Its caplets carry between \(18.3\%\) and \(19.7\%\). With perfect correlation the swaption volatility would be \(18.66\%\). Simulation agrees with the formula within Monte Carlo error (three standard errors plus 1%) at strikes of 2.5%, ATM and 4%.

calibrate_lmm calibrates in two stages. fit_abcd fits the shape to the caplet volatilities, and the \(k_i\) then make every caplet exact. The correlation parameters \((\beta, \rho_\infty)\) are fitted to swaption volatilities through Rebonato's formula, so no simulation is needed.

docs.title: 11.4 Backward-looking rates
docs.text:
Risk-free rates are compounded in arrears, so the coupon \(R_i\) over \([T_i, T_{i+1}]\) is known only at \(T_{i+1}\). Lyashenko and Mercurio's forward market model (ForwardMarketModel) keeps each rate diffusing through its accrual period, with a volatility that decays linearly to zero:

\[ dR_i = \sigma_i(t)\,g_i(t)\,(R_i + \delta)\,dW_i, \qquad g_i(t) = \min\Bigl(1, \frac{(T_{i+1} - t)^+}{T_{i+1} - T_i}\Bigr). \]

Before \(T_i\) it is the forward-looking LMM. A caplet on \(R_i\) is a Black formula to \(T_{i+1}\) with variance \(\int_0^{T_{i+1}}\sigma_i^2 g_i^2\,dt\), which is \(\sigma^2(T_i + \tau_i/3)\) for a flat volatility. A flat 20% on the 4Y×6M period therefore quotes as \(19.25\%\) to the payment date. Even so, the backward-looking caplet is worth more than the forward-looking one, because its variance keeps growing through the accrual period. fmm_paths simulates under the spot measure of the compounded bank account. A rate stays in the drift sum until its accrual ends, and the deflator compounds the realised rates.

docs.title: 11.5 SABR-LMM
docs.text:
SABRLMM gives every forward a SABR smile through a CEV exponent and one stochastic volatility factor for the curve:

\[ dL_i = \alpha_i V_t (L_i + \delta)^\beta\,dW_i, \qquad dV_t = \nu V_t\,dZ_t, \qquad d\langle W_i, Z\rangle = \rho\,dt. \]

Under its own measure each forward is SABR with parameters \((\alpha_i, \beta, \rho, \nu)\), up to a drift on \(V\) from the change of measure. That drift is zero for the first forward. Caplets are therefore priced by Hagan's formula, and sabr_lmm_paths reproduces the smile within Monte Carlo error. The paths use Euler steps with absorption for the forwards and exact lognormal steps for \(V\). Because the volatility factor is shared, swaptions inherit a consistent smile instead of being fitted one by one.

docs.title: 12.1 The contract and lattice engines
docs.text:
A Bermudan swaption can be exercised on any of the dates \(t_1 < \dots < t_m\). Exercising at \(t_k\) enters the remaining co-terminal swap, so the exercise value is \(g_k = (\sum_i a^{(k)}_i P(t_k, t_i))^+\), where \(a^{(k)}\) are that swap's model cashflows. Its value \(\sup_\tau E[D(\tau)g_\tau]\) lies above every co-terminal European and below their sum. bermudan_swaption builds the contract from a Swap, with exercise on the fixing date of each fixed period start after a lockout. coterminal_swaptions returns the matching Europeans with identical dates and underlyings, which is the natural calibration set. On a lattice the value is the dynamic programme \(V(t_k) = \max(g_k, E_{t_k}[D(t_k, t_{k+1})V(t_{k+1})])\).

bermudan_pde solves it on HullWhitePDE or CheyettePDE, with the exercise dates inserted into the time grid. bermudan_tree uses the Hull–White trinomial tree, mapping node rates to the model state by \(x = r - \varphi(t)\). Take a 1Y×5Y payer at 3.5% on 10,000 notional in Hull–White with \(a = 0.05\) and \(\sigma = 1\%\) (3% discounting, 3.4% projection), exercisable annually. The PDE gives \(224.98\), against co-terminal Europeans of \(149.17\), \(168.83\), \(153.91\), \(116.67\) and \(64.60\). With \(\beta = 0.3\) and the same volatility level, Cheyette gives \(223.29\).

docs.title: 12.2 Monte Carlo bounds
docs.text:
lsm implements Longstaff and Schwartz. Regressions of the realised discounted value on basis functions of the state, over in-the-money paths, give a continuation estimate and hence an exercise policy. The policy is then valued on independent paths, which makes the result an unbiased lower bound. ExerciseProblem only needs a transition function, so the code is shared between models. hull_white_exercise_problem uses the exact step hull_white_transition, and cheyette_exercise_problem uses the frozen-volatility step of cheyette_paths.

The dual of Rogers and of Haugh and Kogan bounds the value from above by \(E[\max_k(D(t_k)g_k - M_{t_k})]\) for any martingale with \(M_0 = 0\). andersen_broadie builds \(M\) from the LSM policy itself, with continuation values from nested simulation. The martingale only jumps where the policy exercises, and the width of the gap shows how far the policy is from optimal. For the swaption above, 200,000 paths give a lower bound of \(225.07 \pm 0.53\). With 1,000 outer and 500 inner paths, the upper bound is \(225.16\), a gap of \(0.09\). The PDE value of \(224.98\) lies within the Monte Carlo error of both bounds. A naive policy that exercises as soon as it is in the money is worth only \(194.22\). Its dual bound is \(227.19\), which is still valid but much wider.

docs.title: 13.1 Indices and reference CPI
docs.text:
Price indices are published monthly and used with a lag of \(L\) months. US TIPS, Canadian real return bonds and euro-area linkers interpolate daily between lagged months:

\[ \mathrm{RefCPI}(d) = \mathrm{CPI}_{m-L} + \frac{t-1}{D}\bigl(\mathrm{CPI}_{m-L+1} - \mathrm{CPI}_{m-L}\bigr), \]

for day \(t\) of a month with \(D\) days. InflationIndex implements this, with optional rounding to five places. On 15 January 2023, the October and November 2022 CPI-U levels \(298.012\) and \(297.711\) give TreasuryDirect's \(297.87606\). Zero-coupon swaps on HICP and RPI use the lagged month without interpolation.

docs.title: 13.2 The inflation curve
docs.text: A zero-coupon inflation swap pays \(I(M)/I(S) - 1\) against \((1+K)^n - 1\). Its fair rate depends only on the forward index, so each quote fixes one forward fixing, \(I(S)(1+K)^n\), \(n\) years after the base month. bootstrap_inflation_curve stores these with \(\log I\) linear in months between pillars. A Seasonality multiplies intra-year months by monthly factors that are demeaned to net to zero over a year, so the pillars stay exact. Seasonality.estimate recovers the factors from fixing history. The real discount curve is the value of index-linked money, \(P_r(0,T) = P_n(0,T)\hat I(T)/I(0)\), and real_curve returns it.

docs.title: 13.3 Jarrow–Yildirim
docs.text:
Under the nominal measure, the nominal and real short rates are Hull–White, and the index is lognormal with drift \(n_t - r_t\). The real rate's drift carries \(-\rho_{rI}\sigma_r\sigma_I\), the change of numeraire from real to nominal money. A year-on-year swaplet is worth \(P_n(0,T_1)E^{T_1}[P_r(T_1,T_2)] - P_n(0,T_2)\). Moving \(r_{T_1}\) from the real to the nominal forward measure shifts its mean and gives the convexity factor \(e^{C(T_1,T_2)}\):

\[ C = B_r(T_1,T_2)\Bigl[\rho_{rI}\sigma_r\sigma_I B_r(0,T_1) + \rho_{nr}\sigma_n\sigma_r\int_0^{T_1}e^{-a_r u}B_n(0,u)\,du - \tfrac12\sigma_r^2B_r(0,T_1)^2\Bigr]. \]

This agrees with Mercurio (2005) to \(10^{-15}\). Take \(a_n = 0.1\), \(\sigma_n = 1\%\), \(a_r = 0.05\), \(\sigma_r = 0.8\%\), \(\sigma_I = 1.2\%\) and \((\rho_{nr}, \rho_{nI}, \rho_{rI}) = (0.6, 0.2, -0.3)\), on flat 3% nominal and 1% real curves. The ten-year year-on-year rate is then 2.98 bp below the zero-coupon rate. jy_paths reprices both bond curves and the 9y–10y swaplet within Monte Carlo error, and sits more than eight standard errors from the swaplet without convexity. The log of an index ratio is Gaussian, so year-on-year caplets and zero-coupon caps and floors are Black formulas on the convexity-adjusted forwards. calibrate_jarrow_yildirim fits the volatilities to them. The real-rate volatility enters through the correlations, and the fit has local minima in it. A single start stalls at \(\sigma_r = 0.12\%\), while the default grid of starts recovers \(0.8\%\) to \(10^{-12}\).

docs.title: 13.4 Linked bonds and swaps
docs.text: InflationLinkedBond follows Treasury's conventions. Prices are quoted in real terms at a semiannual real yield, with simple interest over the current period, and the settlement amount is the price plus accrued interest, times the index ratio. Treasury's example, the 3.875% TIPS of January 2009 at a 3.898% real yield, prices at \(99.811030\). On curves, each cash flow is worth \(P_n(0,t)\hat I(t)/I_{\text{base}}\) times its real amount. The principal floor at par is a zero-coupon inflation put struck at the base CPI. For a new ten-year 0.125% bond with the model above, the floor is worth \(0.455\) per 100 when expected inflation is 2% and \(3.204\) when it is 0.25%. ZeroCouponInflationSwap and YearOnYearInflationSwap price the dated swaps. The latter applies the model's convexity on each period after the first.

docs.title: 14.1 Stress testing
docs.text:
curve_price values the InterestRateSwap contracts of spxa.risk on a curve stored in the market dictionary under <rate id>_CURVE. It falls back to a flat curve at r when no curve is stored. The fixed leg pays \(K\) every \(\delta\) years on \(t_k = k\delta\), with a short last period ending at \(T\), and the single-curve floating leg is worth \(1 - P(T)\). Per unit notional the payer swap is worth

\[ V = 1 - P(T) - K\sum_k \tau_k P(t_k), \]

and its DV01 for a parallel rise \(z\) of continuously compounded zero rates is exact:

\[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} = T\,P(T) + K\sum_k \tau_k t_k P(t_k). \]

Against a base market, the change in r shifts the stored curve in parallel. A scenario's rate_shifts_bps therefore moves the whole curve, and curve_pricing_fn plugs a book into StressTestingEngine.

docs.title: 14.2 Key rates from a graph
docs.text:
spxa.graph.rates makes each zero rate \(z_i\) at pillar \(T_i\) an input node, with linear interpolation in zero rate, \(z(t) = \sum_i w_i(t) z_i\). The par rate \(S = (1 - P(T))/A\) of a swap with annuity \(A = \sum_k \tau_k P(t_k)\) has the adjoint

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial z_i} = \frac{T P(T) w_i(T) + S\sum_k \tau_k t_k P(t_k) w_i(t_k)}{A}, \]

so one reverse pass of GradientTape gives every key rate. Because the weights sum to one, the key rates add up to the parallel sensitivity. Take the ESTR curve bootstrapped with MonotoneConvex from the eleven OIS quotes of examples/rates_curve_example.py, with its nodes as pillars. The 10Y annual par rate is \(2.6172\%\), with a sensitivity of \(0.9287\) to the 10Y zero, \(0.0515\) to the 7Y zero and \(1.0293\) in total.

docs.title: Rough Paths and Path Signatures
docs.text:
The signature of a path is the sequence of its iterated integrals. It is a graded, coordinate-free summary that determines the path up to tree-like equivalence (Hambly & Lyons 2010). It also linearises every continuous function of the path: any such function can be approximated by a linear functional of the signature. spxa.signature implements truncated signatures, the shuffle and Lie algebra structure, and the signature kernel computed by solving a Goursat PDE.

Object Implementation Truncated signature \(S^{(M)}(X)\), Chen products spxa.signature.PathSignature Shuffles, log-signature, Witt dimensions spxa.signature.SignatureAlgebra Signature kernel \(\langle S(X), S(Y)\rangle\) spxa.signature.SignatureKernel Graph nodes spxa.graph.signature.PathSignatureNode, SignatureKernelNode, ExpectedSignatureNode, SignatureLinearPricerNode

docs.title: 1. The tensor algebra and the signature
docs.text:
Let \(X:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^d\) have bounded variation. Its signature over \([s,t]\) is the element of the tensor algebra \(T((\mathbb{R}^d)) = \prod_{k\ge0}(\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes k}\)

\[ S(X)_{s,t} = \Big(1,\; \int_{s<u_1<t} dX_{u_1},\; \int_{s<u_1<u_2<t} dX_{u_1}\otimes dX_{u_2},\; \dots\Big). \]

Coordinate \((i_1,\dots,i_k)\) at level \(k\) is \(S^{i_1\cdots i_k}_{s,t} = \int_{s<u_1<\dots<u_k<t} dX^{i_1}_{u_1}\cdots dX^{i_k}_{u_k}\). Truncating at depth \(M\) leaves

\[ \dim T^{(M)}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sum_{k=0}^M d^k = \frac{d^{M+1}-1}{d-1} \]

coordinates (PathSignature.signature_dimension). Levels are stored as flattened arrays in row-major (lexicographic word) order. For example, sig[2].reshape(d, d)[i, j] is \(S^{ij}\).

docs.title: 1.1 Linear segments
docs.text:
For a single linear segment with increment \(\Delta\), every iterated integral can be computed in closed form:

\[ S(\Delta) = \exp_\otimes(\Delta) = \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\Delta^{\otimes k}}{k!}. \]

docs.title: 1.2 Chen's identity
docs.text:
Concatenating paths corresponds to multiplying their signatures in the tensor algebra:

\[ S(X)_{s,u} = S(X)_{s,t}\otimes S(X)_{t,u}, \qquad (A\otimes B)^{(k)} = \sum_{j=0}^k A^{(j)}\otimes B^{(k-j)} . \]

PathSignature.signature evaluates the signature of a piecewise-linear interpolation of the sample points exactly, as the product \(\bigotimes_i \exp_\otimes(\Delta X_i)\). verify_chen_identity checks the identity numerically by splitting a path. No discretisation error is introduced. The only approximation is the piecewise-linear interpolation of the data.

docs.title: 1.3 Properties used in practice
docs.text:
• Invariance under reparametrisation. \(S(X\circ\phi) = S(X)\) for increasing \(\phi\), so the signature ignores the speed at which a path is traversed. To keep time information, add time as an extra coordinate: \(\hat X_t = (t, X_t)\).
  • Uniqueness. Up to tree-like equivalence, \(S(X)\) determines \(X\). For time-augmented paths it determines \(X\) exactly.
  • Universality. On compact sets of paths, linear functionals \(\langle \ell, S(X)\rangle\) are dense in the continuous functions. This is why signature regression works for path-dependent payoffs.
  • Factorial decay. \(\|S^{(k)}(X)\| \le \|X\|_{1\text{-var}}^k / k!\), so truncation error decays super-exponentially in \(M\).

docs.title: 2.1 Shuffle identity
docs.text:
For words \(u, v\), the shuffle product \(u \sqcup\!\sqcup\, v\) is the sum of all interleavings that keep the order within \(u\) and within \(v\) (SignatureAlgebra.shuffles). The signature is a character of the shuffle algebra:

\[ \langle S(X), u\rangle\,\langle S(X), v\rangle = \langle S(X), u \sqcup\!\sqcup\, v\rangle . \]

In particular \(S^i S^j = S^{ij} + S^{ji}\). Products of signature coordinates are therefore again linear in the signature, which is the algebraic basis of universality.

docs.title: 2.2 Group-like elements and the free Lie algebra
docs.text:
Signatures are group-like: \(\log_\otimes S(X)\) lies in the free Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), the space spanned by iterated commutators \([e_i, e_j] = e_i\otimes e_j - e_j\otimes e_i\). Up to level 3,

\[ \log S = S^{(1)} + \Big(S^{(2)} - \tfrac12 S^{(1)}\otimes S^{(1)}\Big) + \Big(S^{(3)} - \tfrac12\big(S^{(1)}\otimes S^{(2)} + S^{(2)}\otimes S^{(1)}\big) + \tfrac13 (S^{(1)})^{\otimes3}\Big) + \cdots \]

For \(d = 2\), SignatureAlgebra.log_signature_2d returns coordinates in the Hall basis:

Level Basis Coordinate 1 \(e_1, e_2\) \(S^1, S^2\) (total increment) 2 \([e_1,e_2]\) Lévy area \(A^{12} = \tfrac12(S^{12}-S^{21})\) 3 \([[e_1,e_2],e_1],\ [[e_1,e_2],e_2]\) \(\tfrac16\langle S^{(3)}, 2\cdot121 - 112 - 211\rangle,\ \tfrac16\langle S^{(3)}, 122 - 2\cdot212 + 221\rangle\)

The level-3 formulas rely on two facts. First, \(\langle S, P\rangle = \langle\log S, P\rangle\) for every Lie polynomial \(P\). Second, the two level-3 basis polynomials are orthogonal, each with squared norm 6. The test suite checks the reconstruction \(\log S^{(3)} = c_1[[e_1,e_2],e_1] + c_2[[e_1,e_2],e_2]\) against the tensor logarithm to machine precision.

docs.title: 2.3 Witt's formula
docs.text:
The dimension of the level-\(k\) component of the free Lie algebra on \(d\) generators is the necklace polynomial

\[ L_d(k) = \frac1k\sum_{m\mid k}\mu(m)\, d^{k/m}, \]

where \(\mu\) is the Möbius function. log_signature_dimension(d, M) returns \(\sum_{k\le M}L_d(k)\). For \(d=2\) the level dimensions are \(2,1,2,3,6,9,18,30,56,99,\dots\), so at depth 10 the log-signature has 226 coordinates against 2046 for the signature.

docs.title: 3. The signature kernel
docs.text:
For paths \(X\) and \(Y\), the signature kernel \(K(X,Y) = \langle S(X), S(Y)\rangle\) (using the inner product induced by the Euclidean inner product on each level) solves a linear hyperbolic Goursat problem (Salvi, Cass, Foster, Lyons & Yang 2021):

\[ \frac{\partial^2 K}{\partial s\,\partial t}(s,t) = \langle \dot X_s, \dot Y_t\rangle\, K(s,t), \qquad K(s,0) = K(0,t) = 1, \]

and \(K(X,Y) = K(T_X, T_Y)\). This is the untruncated inner product, and evaluating it costs \(O(NM\,d)\) for paths with \(N\) and \(M\) segments.

docs.title: 3.1 Discretisation
docs.text:
For piecewise-linear paths, \(\langle\dot X,\dot Y\rangle\) is constant on each grid cell, with cell value \(M_{ij} = \langle\Delta X_i, \Delta Y_j\rangle\) after scaling to unit cells. Integrating the PDE over a cell gives the exact identity

\[ K_{i+1,j+1} - K_{i+1,j} - K_{i,j+1} + K_{i,j} = M_{ij}\cdot\overline{K}_{\text{cell}} . \]

Approximating the cell mean \(\overline K\) by the average of the four corners gives the implicit trapezoidal scheme implemented in SignatureKernel.solve_goursat_pde:

\[ K_{i+1,j+1} = \frac{K_{i+1,j} + K_{i,j+1} - K_{i,j} + \tfrac14 M_{ij}\,(K_{i,j}+K_{i+1,j}+K_{i,j+1})}{1 - \tfrac14 M_{ij}} . \]

The scheme is second-order accurate. For one-dimensional linear paths \(X_t = Y_t = t\) the exact kernel is \(\sum_k 1/(k!)^2 = I_0(2)\). The solver gives \(2.33\) on a single cell, \(2.27994\) on 10 cells and \(2.2795888\) on 100 cells, against \(I_0(2) = 2.2795853\). For coarse samples with large increments, refine the paths dyadically before solving.

docs.title: 3.2 Derived quantities
docs.text:
• Gram matrices. compute_gram_matrix(paths) returns \(G_{ij} = K(X^{(i)}, X^{(j)})\). \(G\) is positive semi-definite, so it can be used directly in kernel ridge regression, SVMs, MMD two-sample tests and Gaussian processes on path space.
  • Feature-space distance. normalized_distance(X, Y) returns $\(\|S(X)-S(Y)\| = \sqrt{K(X,X) - 2K(X,Y) + K(Y,Y)} .\)$ This is a metric on tree-like equivalence classes of paths.
import numpy as np
from spxa.signature import PathSignature, SignatureKernel

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.1, (30, 2)), axis=0)
y = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.1, (40, 2)), axis=0)

ps = PathSignature(depth=10)
truncated = ps.flatten_signature(ps.signature(x)) @ ps.flatten_signature(ps.signature(y))
print(truncated, SignatureKernel.evaluate(x, y))   # agree to ~1e-4 relative

docs.title: 3.3 Expected signature and linear pricing
docs.text:
Universality (§1.3) means a path-dependent payoff can be approximated as \(F(X) \approx \langle \ell, S^{(M)}(\hat X)\rangle\). Expectation is linear, so

\[ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[F(X)] \approx \big\langle \ell,\ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[S^{(M)}(\hat X)]\big\rangle . \]

Once the expected signature has been computed from simulated or model paths (ExpectedSignatureNode), pricing any payoff in the span reduces to a dot product (SignatureLinearPricerNode). The weights \(\ell\) are fitted by regression on sample paths. Under mild conditions the expected signature characterises the law of the path (Chevyrev & Lyons 2016).

docs.title: 4. Relation to rough paths
docs.text: For Brownian paths and other paths with finite \(p\)-variation, \(p \in [2,3)\), the iterated integrals at level 2 are not defined pathwise. Lyons' theory makes them so by lifting \(X\) to a rough path \((X, \mathbb{X})\), where \(\mathbb{X}_{s,t}\) plays the role of \(S^{(2)}_{s,t}\) and Chen's identity is imposed as an axiom. Solutions of rough differential equations then depend continuously on the lift. For Brownian motion the Stratonovich lift \(\mathbb{X}^{ij}_{s,t} = \int_s^t (W^i_u - W^i_s)\circ dW^j_u\) is the limit of the signatures of piecewise-linear interpolations. This limit is exactly what PathSignature computes on sampled data. The antisymmetric part of \(\mathbb{X}\) is the Lévy area, the level-2 log-signature coordinate above.

docs.text:

docs.title: Rough Volatility
docs.text:
Time series of realised volatility behave locally like fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent \(H \approx 0.1\), far below the Brownian value \(H = 1/2\) (Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum 2018). Implied volatility surfaces show the matching signature: the at-the-money skew grows like \(\tau^{H-1/2}\) as maturity \(\tau \to 0\). Classical Markovian stochastic volatility models cannot produce that power law. spxa.rough implements the two reference rough models, rough Bergomi and rough Heston, together with the fractional kernels they are built on.

Object Implementation Power kernels, fBM and Volterra simulation spxa.rough.FractionalKernel Rough Bergomi model spxa.rough.RoughBergomi Rough Heston fractional Riccati solver spxa.rough.FractionalRiccatiSolver Graph nodes spxa.graph.rough.RoughKernelNode, RoughBergomiNode, FractionalRiccatiNode JAX-differentiable variants spxa.diff.simulate_diff_fbm, spxa.diff.simulate_diff_rough_heston

docs.title: 1.1 Fractional Brownian motion
docs.text:
Fractional Brownian motion \(B^H\) is the centred Gaussian process with covariance

\[ \mathbb{E}[B^H_s B^H_t] = \tfrac12\left(s^{2H} + t^{2H} - |t-s|^{2H}\right),\qquad H\in(0,1). \]

It has stationary increments and is self-similar (\(B^H_{ct} \overset{d}{=} c^H B^H_t\)). Its paths are Hölder continuous of every order below \(H\). For \(H < 1/2\) the increments are negatively correlated, and \(B^H\) is neither a semimartingale nor Markov. FractionalKernel.sample_fbm_cholesky samples it exactly on a grid by Cholesky factorisation of this covariance, at \(O(n^3)\) cost.

docs.title: 1.2 Riemann–Liouville (Volterra) processes
docs.text:
Rough volatility models are driven by the Volterra process

\[ \tilde W_t = \int_0^t (t-s)^{H-1/2}\, dZ_s, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\tilde W_t) = \frac{t^{2H}}{2H}, \]

where \(Z\) is a standard Brownian motion. \(\tilde W\) has the same local roughness and scaling as fBM but no longer has stationary increments. What makes it convenient is that it is adapted to \(Z\), so it can be correlated with the Brownian motion that drives the asset price. The joint law of \((\tilde W, Z)\) on a grid is Gaussian, with

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(\tilde W_s, \tilde W_t) &= \frac{s^{a+1}\,t^{a}}{a+1}\;{}_2F_1\!\Big(-a,\,1;\,a+2;\,\tfrac{s}{t}\Big), \qquad s\le t,\ a = H-\tfrac12, \\ \operatorname{Cov}(\tilde W_t, Z_s) &= \frac{t^{a+1} - \big(t-\min(s,t)\big)^{a+1}}{a+1}, \\ \operatorname{Cov}(Z_s, Z_t) &= \min(s,t). \end{aligned} \]

The first line follows from writing \(\int_0^s (s-u)^a (t-u)^a\,du\) as an Euler integral. At \(s=t\) the hypergeometric series converges because \(c-a-b = 2H > 0\). FractionalKernel.volterra_joint_covariance assembles the \(2n\times 2n\) matrix and sample_volterra_cholesky samples it exactly (Bayer, Friz & Gatheral 2016, §4). The test suite checks every entry against direct quadrature.

docs.title: 1.3 Hybrid convolution
docs.text:
FractionalKernel.hybrid_convolution(dw, dt, b_cutoff) evaluates \(\int_0^{t_i}(t_i-s)^{H-1/2}dW_s\) from a given sequence of Brownian increments in \(O(n^2)\):

  • On the \(b\) cells nearest the singularity, it uses the exact cell-average of the kernel, \(\frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{(k-1)\Delta}^{k\Delta} s^{a}\,ds\).
  • On the remaining cells it uses the kernel value at the cell's left endpoint (a Riemann sum).

On the singular cells this is the conditional expectation of the Wiener integral given the increment. That is the best estimate available from dw alone, but it misses the variance of the residual. For \(H = 0.1\) and \(\Delta = 0.01\) it captures about 85% of the true variance \(t^{2H}/2H\). The full Bennedsen–Lunde–Pakkanen (2017) hybrid scheme recovers the missing part by sampling the local Wiener integrals jointly with \(dW\). When exact distributional properties matter, use sample_volterra_cholesky, which is what RoughBergomi does.

docs.title: 2. Rough Bergomi
docs.text:
Bayer, Friz & Gatheral (2016) model the forward variance curve \(\xi_0(t) = \mathbb{E}[v_t]\) as a lognormal Volterra functional:

\[ \begin{aligned} v_t &= \xi_0(t)\,\exp\!\Big(\eta\sqrt{2H}\,\tilde W_t - \tfrac12\eta^2 t^{2H}\Big),\\ \frac{dS_t}{S_t} &= \sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t,\qquad dW_t = \rho\,dZ_t + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,dZ^\perp_t . \end{aligned} \]

Because \(\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{2H}\tilde W_t) = t^{2H}\), the exponential is a mean-one lognormal, so \(\mathbb{E}[v_t] = \xi_0(t)\) holds exactly. RoughBergomi uses a flat curve \(\xi_0(t) \equiv \xi_0\).

docs.title: 2.1 Simulation
docs.text:
RoughBergomi.simulate_paths proceeds in three steps:

  1. Sample \((\tilde W_{t_i}, Z_{t_i})_{i\le n}\) jointly and exactly (§1.2).
  2. Set \(v_{t_i} = \xi_0\exp(\eta\sqrt{2H}\,\tilde W_{t_i} - \tfrac12\eta^2 t_i^{2H})\). This is exact on the grid.
  3. Advance \(\log S\) with a left-point (Itô) Euler step, using \(\Delta W_i = \rho\,\Delta Z_i + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\Delta Z^\perp_i\) where \(\Delta Z_i\) are the increments of the same \(Z\) that drives \(\tilde W\).

Step 3 is what produces the leverage effect: with \(\rho < 0\), returns and variance are negatively correlated. The model has no Markovian state, and exact simulation costs \(O(n^3)\) for the factorisation and \(O(n^2)\) per path. Moderate grids (\(n \lesssim 500\)) are therefore the intended use.

docs.title: 2.2 Short-time ATM skew
docs.text:
To first order in the vol-of-vol, the ATM implied volatility skew is (Fukasawa 2017; Bayer, Friz & Gatheral 2016)

\[ \left.\frac{\partial\sigma_{BS}(k,\tau)}{\partial k}\right|_{k=0} \;\approx\; \frac{\rho\,\eta\,\sqrt{2H}}{2\,(H+\tfrac12)(H+\tfrac32)}\;\tau^{H-1/2}, \qquad \tau\to0 . \]

RoughBergomi.theoretical_short_time_skew(tau) returns the absolute value of this expression. The \(1/(H+\tfrac32)\) factor is the rough-volatility counterpart of the "one-half rule" relating implied and local volatility skews (Bourgey, De Marco, Friz & Pigato 2023). In the test suite, a Monte Carlo estimate of the skew with \(H=0.1\), \(\eta=0.5\), \(\rho=-0.7\), \(\tau = 0.1\) agrees with the asymptotic formula to within about 5–10%. At 60,000 paths the Monte Carlo error dominates, and the test allows 15%.

from spxa.rough import RoughBergomi

model = RoughBergomi(hurst=0.1, eta=1.9, rho=-0.9, xi0=0.04, s0=100.0)
sim = model.simulate_paths(t_mat=1.0, n_steps=100, n_paths=20_000, seed=1)
v, s = sim["variance_paths"], sim["spot_paths"]
print(v.mean(axis=0)[[25, 50, 100]])   # ≈ 0.04 at every date (flat forward variance)
print(s[:, -1].mean())                 # ≈ 100 (martingale)

docs.title: 3. Rough Heston
docs.text:
El Euch & Rosenbaum (2019) introduced a rough version of the Heston model. Let \(\alpha = H + frac12 \in ( frac12, 1]\) and \(X_t = \log(S_t/S_0)\):

\[ egin{aligned} dX_t &= - frac12 V_t\,dt + \sqrt{V_t}\,dW_t,\ V_t &= V_0 + rac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^t (t-s)^{\alpha-1}\Big[\lambda( heta - V_s)\,ds + u\sqrt{V_s}\,dB_s\Big], \qquad d\langle W,B angle_t = ho\,dt . \end{aligned} \]

The model is no longer Markov, but it remains affine. Its characteristic function is

\[ \log\mathbb{E} ig[e^{iuX_T} ig] = \lambda heta\,I^1 h(u,T) + V_0\,I^{1-\alpha}h(u,T), \]

where \(I^ eta f(t) = rac{1}{\Gamma( eta)}\int_0^t (t-s)^{ eta-1}f(s)\,ds\) is the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral and \(h\) solves the fractional Riccati equation

\[ D^\alpha h = F(u,h),\qquad I^{1-\alpha}h(0) = 0, \qquad F(u,h) = - frac12(u^2 + iu) + (i ho u u - \lambda)\,h + frac12 u^2 h^2, \]

or equivalently the Volterra integral equation \(h = I^\alpha F(u,h)\).

docs.title: 3.1 Numerical solution
docs.text:
FractionalRiccatiSolver.solve integrates \(h = I^\alpha F(u,h)\) with the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector of Diethelm, Ford & Freed (2002). On a uniform grid \(t_k = k\Delta\), the predictor is

\[ h^P_{n} = \frac{\Delta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} b_{j,n}\,F(u,h_j), \qquad b_{j,n} = (n-j)^\alpha - (n-1-j)^\alpha, \]

and the corrector is

\[ h_{n} = \frac{\Delta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}\Big(F(u,h^P_{n}) + \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_{j,n}\,F(u,h_j)\Big), \]

with the standard product-trapezoidal weights \(a_{0,n} = (n-1)^{\alpha+1} - (n-1-\alpha)\,n^\alpha\) and \(a_{j,n} = (n-j+1)^{\alpha+1} - 2(n-j)^{\alpha+1} + (n-j-1)^{\alpha+1}\).

docs.title: 3.2 Characteristic function without singular quadrature
docs.text:
The term \(I^{1-\alpha}h\) has a weakly singular kernel. Fractional integrals form a semigroup (\(I^{\beta}I^{\gamma} = I^{\beta+\gamma}\)), and \(h = I^\alpha F\), so

\[ I^{1-\alpha}h = I^{1-\alpha}I^{\alpha}F = I^1 F(u,h) = \int_0^T F(u,h(s))\,ds . \]

rough_heston_char_func therefore evaluates

\[ \log\phi(u,T) = \lambda\theta\int_0^T h(u,s)\,ds + V_0\int_0^T F\big(u,h(u,s)\big)\,ds \]

with the trapezoidal rule. Both integrands are regular, so no singular quadrature is needed. The implementation has three consistency checks:

  • Classical limit. At \(H = \tfrac12\) (\(\alpha = 1\)), \(I^{0}h = h\) and the Riccati equation becomes the Heston ODE \(\psi' = F(u,\psi)\). The solver matches the closed-form Heston characteristic function (spxa.zoo.beyond.heston.HestonProcess.char_func) to about \(10^{-7}\) with 400 steps.
  • Martingale property. At \(u = -i\), \(F(-i, 0) = 0\), so \(h \equiv 0\) and \(\phi(-i,T) = \mathbb{E}[S_T/S_0] = 1\) exactly.
  • Convergence. Results stabilise as the grid is refined, with differences below \(10^{-5}\) between 200 and 400 steps at \(H=0.1\).

Option prices follow from \(\phi\) by standard Fourier inversion, for example the Carr–Madan damped transform used in spxa.analytics.fourier or the Lewis formula.

docs.title: Stochastic Optimal Control
docs.text:
Many problems in quantitative finance are stochastic control problems: choosing a portfolio, liquidating a position, or quoting a two-sided market. A controller steers an SDE to optimise an expected criterion. spxa.control implements the dynamic-programming framework, four canonical problems with closed-form solutions, and a monotone finite-difference HJB solver for problems without them.

Problem Implementation Aliases Abstract problem and Monte Carlo evaluation ControlProblem, ControlledTrajectory Linear–quadratic–Gaussian regulator LinearQuadraticGaussian LQG, LinearQuadraticRegulator Merton consumption–investment MertonPortfolioControl MertonPortfolio, MertonControl, OptimalConsumptionInvestment Almgren–Chriss optimal execution AlmgrenChrissExecution AlmgrenChriss, AlmgrenChrissModel, OptimalExecution Avellaneda–Stoikov market making AvellanedaStoikovMarketMaker AvellanedaStoikov, OptimalMarketMaking, HighFrequencyMarketMaker 1D HJB viscosity solver FiniteDifferenceHJB HJBSolver, HamiltonJacobiBellman, ViscosityHJBSolver

docs.title: 1. Dynamic programming and the HJB equation
docs.text:
A controlled diffusion \(dX_s = \mu(s,X_s,u_s)\,ds + \sigma(s,X_s,u_s)\,dW_s\) with admissible controls \(u_s\in U\) has value function

\[ V(t,x) = \inf_{u}\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^T e^{-\rho(s-t)} f(s,X_s,u_s)\,ds + e^{-\rho(T-t)}g(X_T)\ \Big|\ X_t = x\Big]. \]

Bellman's principle of optimality gives the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

\[ \partial_t V - \rho V + \inf_{u\in U}\Big\{\mu(t,x,u)\,\partial_x V + \tfrac12\sigma^2(t,x,u)\,\partial_{xx}V + f(t,x,u)\Big\} = 0,\qquad V(T,\cdot) = g . \]

For maximisation problems, replace \(\inf\) by \(\sup\). Verification theorem: if a smooth solution exists and the pointwise minimiser \(u^*(t,x)\) gives an admissible feedback control, then \(V\) is the value function and \(u^*\) is optimal. Without classical solutions, \(V\) is the unique viscosity solution under standard comparison conditions (Crandall–Lions; Fleming & Soner 2006).

Each ControlProblem exposes drift, diffusion, running_cost, terminal_cost, optimal_control and value_function. simulate(x0, num_steps, num_paths, seed) runs an Euler–Maruyama Monte Carlo under the feedback policy \(u^*(t,X_t)\) and returns a ControlledTrajectory holding states, controls and realised discounted payoffs. Comparing mean_cost with value_function(0, x0) checks the closed form against simulation.

docs.title: 2. Linear–quadratic–Gaussian control
docs.text:
Consider linear dynamics \(dX = (AX + Bu)\,dt + C\,dW\) with quadratic cost

\[ J(u) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_0^T (X^\top QX + u^\top Ru)\,dt + X_T^\top M X_T\Big], \qquad Q\succeq0,\ R\succ0,\ M\succeq0 . \]

Substituting the ansatz \(V(t,x) = x^\top P(t)x + s(t)\) into the HJB equation gives the backward matrix Riccati equation

\[ -\dot P = PA + A^\top P - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q,\qquad P(T) = M, \]

the optimal linear feedback \(u^*(t,x) = -R^{-1}B^\top P(t)\,x\), and \(s(t) = \int_t^T \operatorname{tr}(CC^\top P(\tau))\,d\tau\). The optimal gain does not depend on the noise \(C\) (certainty equivalence). Noise only adds the constant \(s(t)\). LinearQuadraticGaussian integrates the Riccati ODE backwards. steady_state_riccati solves the continuous algebraic Riccati equation \(PA + A^\top P - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q = 0\), which is the \(T\to\infty\) limit when \((A,B)\) is stabilisable and \((A,Q^{1/2})\) is detectable.

docs.title: 3. Merton's portfolio problem
docs.text:
An agent with wealth \(W\) invests \(\pi_t\) in a risky asset (\(\mu\), \(\sigma\)), keeps the remainder at the risk-free rate \(r\), and consumes at rate \(c_t\):

\[ dW_t = ig[rW_t + \pi_t(\mu - r) - c_t ig]dt + \pi_t\sigma\,dB_t . \]

The agent maximises CRRA utility \(U(c) = c^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\) (\(\gamma>0\), \(\gamma eq1\)) with discount rate \( ho\) and bequest weight \(\varepsilon\):

\[ \sup_{\pi,c}\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^T e^{- ho(s-t)} rac{c_s^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}ds + \varepsilon\,e^{- ho(T-t)} rac{W_T^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}\Big]. \]

Homotheticity reduces the HJB equation to an ODE. Its solution (Merton 1969, 1971) is

\[ rac{\pi^*_t}{W_t} = \alpha^* = rac{\mu - r}{\gamma\sigma^2}, \qquad rac{c^*_t}{W_t} = \kappa(t) = rac{ u}{1 + (\varepsilon^{1/\gamma} u - 1)\,e^{- u(T-t)}}, \qquad V(t,W) = \kappa(t)^{-\gamma}\, rac{W^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}, \]

with

\[ u = rac{ ho - (1-\gamma)\Big(r + rac{(\mu-r)^2}{2\gamma\sigma^2}\Big)}{\gamma}. \]

The Merton fraction \(\alpha^*\) is constant in both time and wealth. As \(T o\infty\), the consumption rate \(\kappa(t)\) tends to \( u\) (infinite_horizon_consumption_propensity). Well-posedness requires \( u > 0\). MertonPortfolioControl.simulate advances log-wealth (a log-Euler step), which keeps wealth strictly positive.

docs.title: 4. Almgren–Chriss optimal execution
docs.text:
The trader liquidates \(Q_0\) shares over \([0,T]\) at trading rate \(v_t = \dot q_t\). Permanent impact moves the price by \(\gamma\,v_t\,dt\) and temporary impact makes the execution price \(\tilde S_t = S_t + \eta v_t\), with \(dS_t = \gamma v_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t\). Minimising the mean–variance criterion \(\mathbb{E}[\text{cost}] + \lambda\operatorname{Var}[\text{cost}]\) over deterministic schedules leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation \(\ddot q = \kappa^2 q\), where

\[ \kappa = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{\eta}} \]

is the urgency. The solution is

\[ q^*(t) = Q_0\frac{\sinh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)},\qquad v^*(t) = -Q_0\kappa\frac{\cosh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}. \]

The expected cost and its variance are

\[ \mathbb{E}[C] = \tfrac12\gamma Q_0^2 + \tfrac12\eta Q_0^2\kappa\,\frac{\sinh(\kappa T)\cosh(\kappa T) + \kappa T}{\sinh^2(\kappa T)}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[C] = \sigma^2 Q_0^2\,\frac{\sinh(2\kappa T) - 2\kappa T}{4\kappa\sinh^2(\kappa T)}. \]

As \(\lambda\to0\), \(q^*\) becomes linear (TWAP, is_twap). Sweeping \(\lambda\) traces the efficient frontier of expected cost against variance (efficient_frontier).

docs.title: 5. Avellaneda–Stoikov market making
docs.text:
A dealer quotes bid and ask prices \(s - \delta^b\) and \(s + \delta^a\) around a mid-price \(dS = \sigma\,dW\). Orders arrive as Poisson processes with intensity \(\lambda(\delta) = A e^{-k\delta}\). The dealer has CARA utility with risk aversion \(\gamma\) over terminal wealth and inventory \(q\). Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008) derive the approximate solution

\[ r(s,q,t) = s - q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t) \qquad\text{(reservation price)}, \] \[ \delta^a + \delta^b = \gamma\sigma^2(T-t) + \frac2\gamma\ln\Big(1 + \frac\gamma k\Big) \qquad\text{(total spread)}, \] \[ \delta^{a} = \tfrac12(\delta^a+\delta^b) - q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t),\qquad \delta^{b} = \tfrac12(\delta^a+\delta^b) + q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t). \]

The quotes are centred on the reservation price, not the mid-price. A long inventory therefore shifts both quotes down, encouraging sells and discouraging buys. The spread does not depend on inventory. optimal_quotes additionally refuses to quote on the side that would exceed max_inventory. Over a step \(\Delta t\) the fill probabilities are \(1 - e^{-\lambda(\delta)\Delta t}\) (fill_probabilities). simulate runs the joint mid-price, fill and inventory dynamics.

docs.title: 6. Finite-difference HJB solver
docs.text:
FiniteDifferenceHJB solves one-dimensional problems of the form in §1 on a grid \(x_i = x_{\min} + i\,\Delta x\), \(t_n = n\,\Delta t\), marching backwards from \(V^N = g\):

\[ V^{n}_i = V^{n+1}_i + \Delta t\Big(\operatorname*{opt}_{u\in\mathcal{U}_h}\big\{\mu\,D^{\pm}V^{n+1}_i + \tfrac12\sigma^2 D^2 V^{n+1}_i + f\big\} - \rho\,V^{n+1}_i\Big), \]

where:

  • \(D^{+}\) (forward difference) is used where \(\mu\ge0\) and \(D^{-}\) (backward difference) where \(\mu<0\) (upwinding);
  • \(D^2\) is the central second difference;
  • \(\mathcal{U}_h\) is a finite set of candidate controls (control_candidates), searched exhaustively at every node.

The scheme is explicit and monotone whenever the CFL-type condition

\[ \Delta t\left(\frac{|\mu|}{\Delta x} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta x^2} + \rho\right) \le 1 \]

holds over all grid points and controls. Monotonicity, stability and consistency together imply convergence to the viscosity solution (Barles & Souganidis 1991). The solver does not enforce this condition. Choose n_time large enough, or the scheme can oscillate and diverge. Boundary nodes use Neumann (zero-gradient) or Dirichlet conditions. value(t, x) and optimal_control(t, x) interpolate the solution off-grid. For a ControlProblem instance, solve_problem(problem) reads the drift, diffusion and costs directly from the problem. The closed-form problems above serve as regression tests for the numerical solver.
