docs.title: Triplet Arithmetic Under Composition
docs.text: This document derives the triplet rules that underpin spxa's operator overloading. Every formula here has a direct code counterpart in spxa/ops/.

docs.title: Addition of independent Lévy processes
docs.text:
Theorem (Sato 1999, Proposition 11.10). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent Lévy processes on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with triplets \((b_X, \Sigma_X, u_X)\) and \((b_Y, \Sigma_Y, u_Y)\) respectively. Then \(Z = X + Y\) is a Lévy process with triplet

\[b_Z = b_X + b_Y, \quad \Sigma_Z = \Sigma_X + \Sigma_Y, \quad u_Z = u_X + u_Y\]

Proof sketch. The characteristic exponent is additive: \(\psi_Z(u) = \psi_X(u) + \psi_Y(u)\), which follows directly from independence and the definition of the characteristic function. Reading off the triplet components from the Lévy–Khintchine form of \(\psi_X + \psi_Y\) gives the result.

This is the core fact that makes spxa's X + Y exact. No approximation is involved for independent Lévy processes.

docs.title: Scalar multiplication
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(X\) has triplet \((b, \sigma^2, u)\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(Z = cX\) has triplet

\[b_Z = cb + \int_{\mathbb{R}} x\left(\mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1} - \mathbf{1}_{\|cx'\| \leq 1} ight) u(dx'/c), \quad \sigma^2_Z = c^2 \sigma^2, \quad u_Z(B) = u(B/c)\]

In the one-dimensional case with the standard truncation, the drift transforms as

\[b_Z = cb + \int_1^{1/|c|} x\, \mathrm{sgn}(c)\, u(dx) \cdot \mathbf{1}_{|c| eq 1}\]

when \(|c| < 1\), and symmetrically when \(|c| > 1\). The image measure \( u_Z(B) = u(B/c)\) is exact in all cases.

Derivation. The characteristic function of \(cX_t\) is \(\mathbb{E}[e^{iucX_t}] = e^{t\psi_X(cu)}\). Substituting \(cu\) for \(u\) in the Lévy–Khintchine formula and changing variables \(x \mapsto x/c\) in the integral gives the result.

docs.title: Linear transformation
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(X\) is a \(d\)-dimensional Lévy process with triplet \((b, \Sigma, u)\) and \(A : \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^k\) is a linear map, then \(Z = AX\) is a \(k\)-dimensional Lévy process with triplet

\[b_Z = Ab + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left(Ax\, \mathbf{1}_{\|Ax\| \leq 1} - Ax\, \mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1} ight) u(dx), \quad \Sigma_Z = A\Sigma A^ op, \quad u_Z = u \circ A^{-1}\]

where \(( u \circ A^{-1})(B) = u(A^{-1}(B))\) is the image measure.

docs.title: Subordination
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(X = (X_t)_{t \geq 0}\) be a Lévy process on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (the parent process) and \(T = (T_t)_{t \geq 0}\) be an independent subordinator — a non-decreasing Lévy process with \(T_0 = 0\). The subordinated process is \(Z_t = X_{T_t}\).

A subordinator has Laplace exponent \(\phi(\lambda) = -\log \mathbb{E}[e^{-\lambda T_1}]\), which is a Bernstein function: \(\phi(\lambda) = \delta \lambda + \int_0^\infty (1 - e^{-\lambda s})\, \rho(ds)\) with \(\delta \geq 0\) and \(\rho\) the Lévy measure of \(T\) (a measure on \((0, \infty)\) with \(\int (1 \wedge s)\, \rho(ds) < \infty\)).

Theorem (Sato 1999, Theorem 30.1; Cont & Tankov 2004, Proposition 4.4). \(Z = X \circ T\) is a Lévy process with characteristic exponent

\[\psi_Z(u) = -\phi(-\psi_X(u)) = \delta \psi_X(u) + \int_0^\infty \left(e^{s\psi_X(u)} - 1\right) \rho(ds)\]

The triplet of \(Z\) in one dimension is:

\[b_Z = \delta b_X + \int_0^\infty \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} x\, e^{s\psi_X}\, \text{(via inversion)}\right) \rho(ds)\]

In practice, computing the triplet of \(Z\) explicitly requires either a closed-form inversion (available for named process pairs like BM-under-Gamma = Variance Gamma) or numerical evaluation of the Lévy measure via

\[\nu_Z(B) = \delta \nu_X(B) + \int_0^\infty P(X_s \in B)\, \rho(ds)\]

spxa computes subordination exactly for known pairs (documented per process) and falls back to numerical quadrature otherwise, with ExactnessLevel.MOMENT_PROPAGATION and an explicit warning.

The @ operator in spxa. Z = X @ T denotes subordination: \(Z_t = X_{T_t}\). The left operand is the parent process, the right operand must be a subordinator.

docs.title: Cumulant propagation under composition
docs.text:
For any operation producing a Lévy process, cumulants follow from the triplet:

\[\kappa_n(Z_t) = t \cdot \kappa_n(Z_1) = t \cdot \int x^n\, \nu_Z(dx) + t \cdot \sigma_Z^2 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{n=2}\]

This is computed symbolically by spxa when \(\nu_Z\) has a closed-form density, and numerically otherwise with a stated error bound.

docs.title: Property propagation
docs.text:
Operations propagate properties through the lattice defined in spxa/core/properties.py. Key rules:

Property Under \(X + Y\) Under \(cX\) Under \(X \circ T\) Stationary increments preserved preserved preserved Independent increments preserved preserved preserved Finite variance preserved if both have it preserved depends on \(T\) Finite mean preserved if both have it preserved preserved if \(T\) has finite mean Self-similarity index \(H\) lost unless \(X = Y\) preserved lost in general Martingale preserved if both are preserved if \(c \neq 0\) and \(b=0\) depends Tail index \(\alpha\) \(\min(\alpha_X, \alpha_Y)\) preserved depends on \(T\)

Cells marked "depends" cause spxa to check the specific triplet values rather than propagating symbolically.

docs.title: What breaks outside the Lévy regime
docs.text:
The above arithmetic is exact only for independent Lévy processes. The following cases require approximation:

  • Fractional Brownian motion: not a semimartingale, not a Lévy process, no triplet. The Hurst index \(H\) is the relevant parameter; self-similarity and long memory are propagated heuristically.
  • Products \(X \cdot Y\): not a Lévy process in general even for Lévy \(X\), \(Y\). spxa computes moments of the product when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent using the moment product formula.
  • Stochastic integrals \(\int f(X_s)\, dY_s\): exact only for deterministic \(f\); for random integrands, Itô isometry gives the variance and spxa propagates moments only.

In all approximate cases, ExactnessLevel is set to MOMENT_PROPAGATION or SIMULATION_ONLY, and calling .triplet raises ExactnessError with an explanation.

docs.title: Volatility
docs.text:
spxa.vol builds implied-volatility surfaces that are free of static arbitrage, and calibrates models to them.

  • §1–7 cover the parametric layer, from SVI slices, SSVI and eSSVI through calibration, interpolation in time and the risk-neutral distributions they imply, up to the surface object built from option quotes.
  • §8–10 cover the models consistent with a surface: local volatility, stochastic local volatility, and rough Heston and rough Bergomi with the VIX.
  • §11–13 cover what a surface does not pin down: model-free bounds by martingale optimal transport, variance and volatility swaps, and the model risk of exotics.
  • §14 connects the package to stress testing, the process zoo and computational graphs.

docs.title: 1. Coordinates and static arbitrage
docs.text:
Surfaces are written in log-forward moneyness and total implied variance,

\[ k = \log\frac{K}{F_T}, \qquad w(k, T) = \sigma_{\text{BS}}^2(k, T)\,T, \]

and the undiscounted call price over the forward is \(c(k, w) = \Phi(d_+) - e^k\Phi(d_-)\) with \(d_\pm = -k/\sqrt w \pm \sqrt w/2\).

Butterfly arbitrage. A slice \(w(k)\) is free of butterfly arbitrage if and only if the density of \(X = \log(S_T/F_T)\),

\[ p(k) = \frac{g(k)}{\sqrt{2\pi w(k)}}\,e^{-d_-(k)^2/2}, \qquad g(k) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{k w'}{2w}\Bigr)^2 - \frac{w'^2}{4}\Bigl(\frac1w + \frac14\Bigr) + \frac{w''}{2}, \]

is non-negative and call prices vanish as \(k \to \infty\) (Gatheral & Jacquier 2014, Lemma 2.2). Here \(g\) is Durrleman's function. check_butterfly scans \(g\) on a grid and reports its minimum and the intervals where it is negative.

Calendar arbitrage. With proportional dividends, a surface is free of calendar-spread arbitrage if and only if \(T \mapsto w(k, T)\) is non-decreasing for every \(k\) (Lemma 2.1). check_calendar reports the worst decrease between consecutive slices.

Wings. Lee's moment formula links the wing slopes \(\beta_R = \limsup_{k\to\infty} w/k\) and \(\beta_L = \limsup_{k\to-\infty} w/|k|\) to the critical moments \(\tilde p = \sup\{p : E[S^{1+p}] < \infty\}\) and \(\tilde q = \sup\{q : E[S^{-q}] < \infty\}\):

\[ \beta = 2 - 4\bigl(\sqrt{x^2 + x} - x\bigr), \qquad x = \frac{(2 - \beta)^2}{8\beta}, \]

so no wing can be steeper than 2. With \(w \approx \beta|k|\), the density above decays like \(e^{-\lambda|k|}\) with \(\lambda_R = 1 + \tilde p\) and \(\lambda_L = \tilde q\). The tests check both rates from log-density slopes at \(|k| = 2000\) to \(4000\). They also show that \(E[S^{1+p}]\) converges just below \(\tilde p\) and diverges just above it. Separately, an arbitrage-free surface has \(|\partial_k w| \le 4\) (Rogers & Tehranchi 2010).

docs.title: 2. SVI slices
docs.text:
The raw SVI slice of Gatheral (2004) is

\[ w(k) = a + b\Bigl(\rho(k - m) + \sqrt{(k - m)^2 + \sigma^2}\Bigr), \]

with minimum \(a + b\sigma\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\) at \(k^* = m - \rho\sigma/\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\) and wing slopes \(b(1 \pm \rho)\). The natural parametrisation \((\Delta, \mu, \rho, \omega, \zeta)\) maps to raw SVI by

\[ a = \Delta + \tfrac{\omega}{2}(1 - \rho^2), \quad b = \tfrac{\omega\zeta}{2}, \quad m = \mu - \rho/\zeta, \quad \sigma = \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}/\zeta. \]

The jump-wings parametrisation \((v_t, \psi_t, p_t, c_t, \tilde v_t)\) uses the ATM variance, ATM skew, put and call wing slopes and minimum variance, all of which scale sensibly across expiries.

Not every raw SVI slice is arbitrage-free. Axel Vogt's slice \((a, b, \rho, m, \sigma) = (-0.0410, 0.1331, 0.3060, 0.3586, 0.4153)\) has \(\min g = -0.032864\) at \(k = 0.879\). Its jump-wings parameters at \(t = 1\) are \((0.01742625, -0.1752111, 0.6997381, 1.316798, 0.0116249)\), as in Gatheral & Jacquier (2014, Example 3.1). There are two repairs:

  • Projection (Gatheral & Jacquier, §5.1). Keep \((v, \psi, p)\) and set \(c' = p + 2\psi\) and \(\tilde v' = 4vpc'/(p + c')^2\). The result is an SSVI slice with the same ATM level and skew. For Vogt's slice \(c' = 0.3493158\).
  • Constrained fit. calibrate_svi_butterfly_free imposes \(g \ge 10^{-8}\) on a grid. Wherever \(g\) dips between grid nodes, it adds cutting planes at the local minima. Refitting Vogt's slice on 61 points of \([-1.5, 1.5]\) gives an arbitrage-free slice with rmse \(0.00231\) in total variance.

calibrate_svi is the quasi-explicit method of Zeliade and De Marco & Martini. For fixed \((m, \sigma)\) the slice is linear in \((a, b\sigma, \rho b\sigma)\) on a box, so the inner problem is an exact bounded least-squares solve and only \((m, \sigma)\) are searched. It recovers Vogt's raw parameters exactly from noiseless quotes.

docs.title: 3. SSVI and eSSVI
docs.text:
SSVI (Gatheral & Jacquier 2014) writes the whole surface through the ATM total variance \(\theta_t\):

\[ w(k, \theta_t) = \frac{\theta_t}{2}\Bigl(1 + \rho\varphi(\theta_t)k + \sqrt{(\varphi(\theta_t)k + \rho)^2 + 1 - \rho^2}\Bigr). \]

The surface is free of calendar arbitrage when \(\theta_t\) is non-decreasing and \(0 \le \partial_\theta(\theta\varphi) \le \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}}{\rho^2}\varphi\) (Theorem 4.1). It is free of butterfly arbitrage when \(\theta\varphi(1 + |\rho|) < 4\) and \(\theta\varphi^2(1 + |\rho|) \le 4\) (Theorem 4.2). The Heston-like curvature \(\varphi(\theta) = \frac{1}{\lambda\theta}\bigl(1 - \frac{1 - e^{-\lambda\theta}}{\lambda\theta}\bigr)\) is arbitrage-free for \(\lambda \ge (1 + |\rho|)/4\). The power law \(\varphi(\theta) = \eta\theta^{-\gamma}(1 + \theta)^{\gamma - 1}\) is arbitrage-free for \(\gamma \le 1/2\) and \(\eta(1 + |\rho|) \le 2\). calibrate_ssvi fits \(\rho\), the curvature parameters and \(\theta_t\) under these constraints. It recovers \((\rho, \eta, \gamma) = (-0.7, 1.1, 0.4)\) and the Heston-like \((\rho, \lambda) = (-0.6, 2)\) to about \(10^{-7}\).

eSSVI (Hendriks & Martini) gives each expiry its own \((\theta, \psi, \rho)\) with \(\psi = \theta\varphi\). The butterfly conditions become \(\psi(1 + |\rho|) < 4\) and \(\psi^2(1 + |\rho|) \le 4\theta\). Two slices are free of calendar arbitrage when

\[ \theta_2 \ge \theta_1, \qquad \psi_2 \ge \psi_1, \qquad |\rho_2\psi_2 - \rho_1\psi_1| \le \psi_2 - \psi_1, \]

which spxa uses as a sufficient condition. calibrate_essvi follows Corbetta, Cohort, Laachir & Martini (2019). Each slice is anchored at the quote \((k^*, \theta^*)\) closest to the money, through the exact relation

\[ \theta = \frac{(2\theta^* - \rho\psi k^*)^2 - \psi^2 k^{*2}}{4\theta^*}. \]

The fit then scans \(\rho\) and solves for \(\psi\) within the closed-form bounds implied by the butterfly and calendar conditions. Between expiries, \(\theta\), \(\psi\) and \(\rho\psi\) are interpolated linearly in time, which preserves both conditions. The tests recover the published SPX slices of Corbetta et al. (Table 1) to about \(10^{-9}\).

docs.title: 4. Surfaces of SVI slices
docs.text:
calibrate_svi_surface fits raw SVI slices from the shortest expiry upwards, in the spirit of Gatheral & Jacquier (§5). Each slice must satisfy Durrleman's condition and stay above the previous slice on a common grid, \(w_i(k_j) \ge w_{i-1}(k_j)\). Both constraints are refined with cutting planes. The wing slopes must also be ordered, \(b_i(1 \pm \rho_i) \ge b_{i-1}(1 \pm \rho_{i-1})\), which prevents crossings beyond the grid. When the quotes themselves cross, the shorter slice is kept and the longer one is fitted as closely as the constraints allow. Slices taken from an arbitrage-free SSVI surface are reproduced to \(5 \times 10^{-7}\).

Interpolation in time. PriceInterpolatedSurface interpolates prices rather than variances (Gatheral & Jacquier, §5.3). Take \(\theta_t\) linear in \(t\) between the ATM nodes, starting from \(\theta_0 = 0\). For \(t_i \le t \le t_{i+1}\), set

\[ c(k, t) = \alpha_t\,c_i(k) + (1 - \alpha_t)\,c_{i+1}(k), \qquad \alpha_t = \frac{\sqrt{\theta_{i+1}} - \sqrt{\theta_t}}{\sqrt{\theta_{i+1}} - \sqrt{\theta_i}}. \]

Below the first expiry, \(c_0(k) = (1 - e^k)^+\) is intrinsic value. A convex combination of call-price functions is the call-price function of a mixture of distributions, so butterfly arbitrage cannot appear. Because \(\alpha_t\) decreases in \(t\) and the slices are ordered, prices are non-decreasing in \(t\), so calendar arbitrage cannot appear either. In \(s = \sqrt\theta\) the ATM price is \((s - s^3/24 + \dots)/\sqrt{2\pi}\), and the weights are linear in \(s\). The only error comes from interpolating \(s^3\) linearly, which is exactly \((s - s_i)(s_{i+1} - s)(s_i + s + s_{i+1})\). The interpolated ATM total variance therefore falls short of \(\theta_t\) by

\[ \theta_t - w(0, t) = \frac{s}{12}(s - s_i)(s_{i+1} - s)(s_i + s + s_{i+1})\bigl(1 + O(\theta_{i+1})\bigr), \qquad s = \sqrt{\theta_t}. \]

The tests check this to a relative accuracy of \(\theta_{i+1}/20\).

docs.title: 5. Implied distributions
docs.text:
ImpliedDistribution turns a slice into the law of \(X = \log(S_T/F_T)\). Differentiating the call price along the slice gives the survival function, which is also the price of a normalised digital call:

\[ \mathbb{Q}(X > k) = \Phi(d_-) - \varphi(d_-)\,\frac{w'(k)}{2\sqrt{w}}. \]

Together with the density of §1, this is exact in \(w\), \(w'\) and \(w''\). Moments, the forward ratio \(E[e^X]\), call repricing, quantiles and inverse-transform samples are built on top. The integration range is widened until the exact tail mass beyond it is below \(10^{-17}\). For an arbitrage-free slice the tests find unit mass and \(E[e^X] = 1\) to \(10^{-11}\), and they reprice calls by quadrature to the same accuracy. A slice with butterfly arbitrage shows up as a cdf that decreases somewhere; quantiles and samples refuse such slices.

docs.title: 6.1 Forwards and quotes
docs.text:
build_vol_surface takes bid/ask chains, one per expiry, and fits a surface in four steps:

  1. Forward and discount factor. Each expiry's forward \(F_i\) and discount factor \(D_i\) come from the chain if set. Otherwise they are implied from put-call parity, \(C - P = D(F - K)\), by a robust line fit across strikes.
  2. Term structure. ForwardTermStructure interpolates \(\log F\) and \(\log D\) linearly in \(t\) between expiries, which means constant carry and flat discount forwards. It starts from \((0, \log S)\) when the spot is known.
  3. Total variances. chain_total_variance converts the out-of-the-money mids to \((k, w)\) pairs and drops quotes that break the price bounds. Weights are uniform, by vega, or from the bid-ask spread.
  4. Fit. The pairs are fitted with calendar-free SVI (§4), eSSVI or SSVI (§3).

The result is a SurfaceBuild holding a VolSurface and the fitted data. SurfaceBuild.quality() reports the following per expiry, together with a calendar check across expiries:

  • the RMSE and largest implied-volatility error;
  • ATM volatility and skew;
  • the minimum of Durrleman's \(g\) (§1).

docs.title: 6.2 Repairing prices
docs.text:
Some quotes cannot be fitted without arbitrage at all. Cohen, Reisinger & Wang (2020) work in normalised units \(c = C/(DF)\) and \(\kappa = K/F\). A grid then extends to an arbitrage-free surface, linear in \(\kappa\) between quotes, exactly when four conditions hold:

  • \((1 - \kappa)^+ \le c \le 1\);
  • slopes lie in \([-1, 0]\), with \(c(0) = 1\);
  • slopes are non-decreasing (no butterfly arbitrage);
  • \(c\) is non-decreasing in \(T\) at every strike of either slice inside both ranges.

All four conditions are linear in the prices. repair_call_prices therefore finds the smallest weighted \(\ell^1\) change with a linear programme, and moves that stay inside the bid-ask spread can be made free. For \(F = 100\), \(D = 1\) and calls 13, 8 and 2 at strikes 90, 100 and 110, the slopes \(-0.5\) and \(-0.6\) break convexity. The cheapest repair lowers the middle price to 7.5, an \(\ell^1\) change of \(0.005\) in normalised units.

docs.title: 6.3 Smoothing prices
docs.text:
Fengler (2009) fits a natural cubic spline \(g(\kappa)\) to normalised call prices by quadratic programming:

\[ \min_{g,\,\gamma}\ \sum_i w_i\bigl(y_i - g(u_i)\bigr)^2 + \lambda\,\gamma^\top R\,\gamma, \]

Here \(\gamma = g''\) at the knots, so \(\gamma \ge 0\) makes \(g\) convex. The spline must also satisfy \((1 - u)^+ \le g \le 1\). fengler_surface fits the longest expiry first and each shorter one under \(g_{T_1} \le g_{T_2}\). Imposing this only at the knots leaves small violations between them. Instead, each spline piece is written in Bernstein form on the union of both knot sets, halved, and every Bernstein coefficient of the difference is constrained. The difference then stays non-negative to below \(10^{-12}\) everywhere on the overlap.

docs.title: 7.1 Strikes, volatilities and time interpolation
docs.text:
VolSurface(model, forward) combines a total-variance model with a forward curve. It works in strikes: prices, implied volatilities, deltas and the smile at each expiry, all broadcasting \(K\) against \(T\). The forward variance between two expiries at fixed \(k\) is \(\bigl(w(k, T_2) - w(k, T_1)\bigr)/(T_2 - T_1)\). It is non-negative for every \(k\) exactly when there is no calendar arbitrage, and forward_vol raises otherwise.

VolSurface.from_slices interpolates between fitted slices, in one of three ways:

Mode Interpolates Guarantee price (default) \(c(k, t)\), by §4 no static arbitrage if the slices have none fixed_k \(w(k, t)\) linearly in \(t\) at fixed \(k\) no calendar arbitrage if the slices are ordered normalised \(w/\theta_t\) at fixed \(x = k/\sqrt{\theta_t}\), with \(\theta_t\) linear exact for SSVI with \(\varphi(\theta)\sqrt\theta\) constant

Only the variance modes extrapolate beyond the last expiry. In the normalised mode \(w_i(x\sqrt{\theta_i})/\theta_i\) is the same function of \(x\) on every slice of such an SSVI surface. The interpolation then returns the SSVI surface itself at every intermediate \(\theta_t\).

docs.title: 7.2 Delta conventions
docs.text:
The Black forward delta of a call is \(N(d_1)\), and with premium adjustment it is \((K/F)N(d_2)\). strike_from_delta inverts either convention at the slice's own volatility. The premium-adjusted call delta is not monotone in \(K\), so it is inverted on the branch above its maximum. The ATM delta-neutral straddle strike solves call delta + put delta \(= 0\). At a fixed volatility this is \(Fe^{w/2}\), or \(Fe^{-w/2}\) with premium adjustment. For \(F = 100\), \(\sigma = 20\%\) and \(T = 1\) these are 102.0201 and 98.0199, and the 25-delta call strike is \(F\exp\bigl(\sigma N^{-1}(0.75) + w/2\bigr) = 116.7539\).

Under a smile, the forward delta depends on how \(\sigma\) moves with the forward. Sticky strike keeps Black's delta. Sticky moneyness, \(\sigma = \sigma(\log(K/F))\), gives \(\Delta = \Delta_{BS} - \mathcal V_{BS}\,\sigma_k/F\). Under a negative skew this sticky-moneyness delta is the larger of the two.

docs.title: 7.3 Bumps and bucketed vega
docs.text:
A bump adds \(\delta(k, T)\) to the implied volatility at fixed log-moneyness, \(w' = (\sigma + \delta)^2T\). There are three shapes:

  • parallel_bump is \(\delta = s\);
  • skew_bump is \(\delta = sk\), which raises the ATM skew by exactly \(s\);
  • expiry_buckets are triangular hats in \(T\) on pillar expiries that sum to one. A book at 0.75 years with pillars at 0.5 and 1 year therefore splits its vega equally between them.

bucketed_vega reprices any function of a surface under central bumps. The bucketed vegas add up to the parallel vega to first order.

docs.title: 7.4 Simulation and persistence
docs.text: VolSurface.terminal_distribution(T) is the implied law of \(\log(S_T/F_T)\) (§5), and sample_terminal draws \(S_T\) by inverse transform. Monte Carlo then reprices the forward, calls and digitals to within four standard errors, which checks the surface end to end. dumps and loads serialise surfaces, models, forwards and curves to JSON, with a type tag on each object. The round trip is bit-exact, because JSON writes each float as the shortest decimal that reads back to it.

docs.title: 8.1 Dupire's formula in implied variance
docs.text:
Dupire (1994) showed that exactly one diffusion \(dS_t = (r - q)S_t\,dt + \sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}(S_t, t)S_t\,dW_t\) reproduces a given arbitrage-free call surface. In log-forward moneyness \(y = \log(K/F_T)\) and total implied variance \(w(y, T)\) the formula reads (Gatheral, 2006)

\[ \sigma^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(K, T) = \frac{\partial_T w}{1 - \dfrac{y}{w}\,\partial_y w + \dfrac14\Bigl(-\dfrac14 - \dfrac1w + \dfrac{y^2}{w^2}\Bigr)(\partial_y w)^2 + \dfrac12\,\partial_{yy} w}. \]

Rates and dividends drop out because strikes are measured against the forward. The denominator is Durrleman's \(g\) (§1), and the numerator is the forward variance at fixed moneyness (§7.1). The local variance is therefore positive exactly where the surface is free of butterfly and calendar arbitrage. LocalVolSurface returns nan elsewhere: if \(w = (0.04T - 0.02T^2)\) at every \(y\), the local vol is \(\sqrt{0.02}\) at \(T = 1/2\) and undefined at \(T = 1.5\). VolSurface.local_vol evaluates the formula with five-point differences of any surface. LocalVolGrid tabulates it for fast lookups.

As \(T \to 0\), the implied vol is the harmonic mean of the local vol between spot and strike (Berestycki, Busca & Florent, 2002):

\[ \frac{1}{\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}(k)} = \int_0^1 \frac{du}{\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}(uk)}. \]

bbf_implied_vol evaluates this integral. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}} = a + by\) it gives \(bk/\log(1 + bk/a)\). Differentiating at \(k = 0\) gives the familiar rule that the short-dated local skew is twice the implied skew: for a time-independent smile \(\sigma(k) = 0.2 - 0.1k\), the ATM local skew tends to \(-0.2\).

docs.title: 8.2 Pricing under local volatility
docs.text: A LocalVolSurface is a volatility function \(\sigma(S, t)\) for the solvers of PDE methods. dupire_pde solves the forward Dupire equation for all strikes and expiries at once, and must give back the surface it came from. black_scholes_pde, american and barrier price backwards, one contract at a time. Two checks tie the two directions together: the forward and backward vanilla prices converge to the surface, and down-and-out plus down-and-in equals the vanilla. With \(q = 0\) an American call under local vol is worth its European value, as it is under any diffusion.

docs.title: 8.3 Andreasen–Huge interpolation
docs.text:
Dupire's formula needs a smooth, arbitrage-free surface. Andreasen & Huge (2011) start from the quotes instead. They take \(\vartheta(x, t)\) piecewise constant in normalised strike \(x = K/F_t\), with one level per quote, and advance normalised calls \(c(x, t)\) over each expiry interval with one fully implicit step:

\[ \Bigl[I - \tfrac12 (t_i - t_{i-1})\,\vartheta_i^2(x)\,x^2 D_{xx}\Bigr] c_i = c_{i-1}. \]

The matrix is an M-matrix, so \(c_i\) stays convex in \(x\), within \((1 - x)^+ \le c \le 1\), and \(c_i \ge c_{i-1}\). The surface is free of static arbitrage by construction, between expiries as well, where the same step is taken with a partial time step. calibrate_andreasen_huge fits the levels expiry by expiry, and reproduces arbitrage-free quotes to solver tolerance.

docs.title: 8.4 Monte Carlo and the forward smile
docs.text: local_vol_paths simulates \(\log S\) by Euler steps on a LocalVolGrid, storing only the requested times. Forward-start options pay \((S_{T_2}/S_{T_1} - k)^+\) at \(T_2\). Their value depends on the joint law of \(S_{T_1}\) and \(S_{T_2}\), which the surface does not determine. LocalVolPaths.forward_start prices them under local vol. Put–call parity holds path by path: call minus put pays \(S_{T_2}/S_{T_1} - k\), and its expectation is \(e^{-rT_2}\bigl(e^{(r - q)(T_2 - T_1)} - k\bigr)\). With a constant volatility the price is \(e^{-rT_1}\) times a Black–Scholes call on unit spot, with strike \(k\), expiry \(T_2 - T_1\) and the same \(r\) and \(q\).

docs.title: 8.5 Densities and diagnostics
docs.text:
By Gyöngy's theorem, the marginal laws of the local-vol diffusion are those implied by the surface. LocalVolSurface.density solves the Fokker–Planck equation of \(\log S\) with FokkerPlanck1D and returns the density of \(y = \log(S_T/F_T)\). It matches the Breeden–Litzenberger density \(e^{rT}\partial_{KK}C\) (§5), keeps unit mass, and keeps \(E[S_T] = F_T\).

local_vol_diagnostics combines these checks for a given surface. It maps where the local vol is undefined on a (moneyness, time) grid. If it is defined everywhere, it reprices a strike × expiry grid with one forward Dupire solve and reports the implied-vol errors, which shrink as the grid is refined. For an SSVI surface whose \(\theta_t = 0.04t - 0.012t^2\) peaks at \(t = 5/3\), a 40-step time grid to \(t = 2\) first flags undefined points at \(t = 1.7\).

docs.title: 9.1 The model
docs.text:
Local volatility fits every vanilla but implies a forward smile that flattens too quickly. Stochastic volatility has realistic dynamics but cannot fit the whole surface. SLV combines the two. In forward log-moneyness \(y = \log(S_t/F_t)\),

\[ dy = -\tfrac12 L^2(t, y)\,v\,dt + L(t, y)\sqrt v\,dW^1, \qquad dv = \kappa(\theta - v)\,dt + \eta\,\xi\sqrt v\,dW^2, \qquad d\langle W^1, W^2\rangle = \rho\,dt, \]

with a Heston variance (Heston, priced in forward coordinates by Lewis's integral; in 't Hout and Foulon's case 1 gives \(8.8948693600540\)) and a leverage function \(L\). The mixing fraction \(\eta \in [0, 1]\) scales the vol-of-variance. By Gyöngy's theorem, the marginals of \(y\), and therefore all vanillas, are those of local volatility if and only if

\[ L^2(t, y)\,E[v_t \mid y_t = y] = \sigma_{LV}^2(t, y). \]

The leverage depends on the model's own conditional expectation, so the model is a McKean nonlinear diffusion, and calibrating it means solving for that conditional expectation.

docs.title: 9.2 The forward equation
docs.text: slv_forward evolves the joint density \(p(t, y, v)\) from a delta at \((0, v_0)\). As in the one-dimensional FokkerPlanck1D, the forward operator is the discrete adjoint \(W^{-1}A_j^{\mathsf T}W\) of each part of the backward ADI splitting of spxa.pde, where \(W\) holds the control-volume areas. Every generator row sums to zero, so the mass is conserved to rounding. The degenerate edge \(v = 0\) is "natural". The far edges in \(y\) and the top of the variance grid are absorbing: with a natural condition on a non-degenerate edge, the adjoint scheme blows up. slv_grid clusters variance nodes towards zero, places \(v_0\) on a node, and takes the top of the grid at the \(1 - 10^{-6}\) non-central chi-square quantile of \(v_t\) over the horizon. With \(L \equiv 1\) the density reproduces the Heston smile within 5 bp on a \(121 \times 61\) grid with 100 steps, and within 1.5 bp on \(161 \times 81\) with 200 steps.

docs.title: 9.3 Calibration by forward induction
docs.text: calibrate_leverage reads \(E[v \mid y]\) from the current density at each step, sets \(L^2 = \sigma_{LV}^2/E[v \mid y]\) with the local variance at the step midpoint, and advances the density with that leverage (Ren, Madan & Qian). Where the marginal density is negligible, the conditional expectation is extended flat. Calibrated to the SSVI surface of §8, the model reprices the smile at one year within 5 bp at \(\eta = 0.5\) on the \(121 \times 61\) grid, and within 2.5 bp at \(\eta = 1\) on \(161 \times 81\). The local variance must be tabulated finely in \(y\) (as_local_vol uses 601 points): linear interpolation of a convex function biases the volatility upwards. As a consistency check, feeding the model its own Gyöngy local variance returns \(L \equiv 1\) to \(10^{-9}\).

docs.title: 9.4 Particles, Monte Carlo and the PDE
docs.text: calibrate_leverage_particles is the particle method of Guyon and Henry-Labordère. It simulates \(N\) particles and estimates \(E[v \mid y]\) at each step by Gaussian kernel regression, with bandwidth \(\propto \sigma\sqrt t\,N^{-1/5}\). On the same problem its leverage agrees with the forward equation's within 2.5%. slv_paths simulates the calibrated model with full-truncation Euler for \(v\) and a log-Euler step for \(y\), so \(e^y\) is an exact martingale step by step. Knock-out barriers are monitored continuously through the Brownian-bridge survival probability \(1 - e^{-2d_0d_1/(a^2\Delta t)}\). In the Black–Scholes limit this matches Reiner–Rubinstein at 20 steps, while discrete monitoring overprices by more than five standard errors. SLVPDE prices backwards in \((S, v)\). Its far spot edge uses the linearity condition, which is exact for payoffs linear in \(S\) (in log-spot the same condition breaks put–call parity). Spot barriers become zero-Dirichlet edges. The PDE and Monte Carlo agree on calibrated-SLV barriers within three standard errors.

docs.title: 9.5 The mixing fraction
docs.text: Every \(\eta\) reprices the same vanillas, but path-dependent prices move. At \(\eta = 0\) the variance is deterministic and the model is local volatility: a one-year down-and-out call (spot and strike 100, barrier 85, \(r = 3\%\), \(q = 1\%\)) on the SSVI surface agrees with the one-factor local-vol PDE value \(8.18\) within 0.2%. A one-year up-and-out call with barrier 130 is worth \(5.80\), \(6.00\) and \(6.33\) at \(\eta = 0\), \(0.5\) and \(1\), while the smile is matched within 6 bp in each case. calibrate_slv builds the model for a given \(\eta\) from a local-vol surface or a VolSurface. In practice \(\eta\) is set from barrier or forward-start quotes, which the vanillas cannot pin down.

docs.title: 10.1 Rough Heston
docs.text:
Realised volatility is rough: its log increments behave like fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index \(H \approx 0.1\). Implied volatility shows the same roughness, with an at-the-money skew that grows like \(T^{H - 1/2}\) as \(T o 0\). A classical diffusion gives a flat skew there. In the rough Heston model (El Euch & Rosenbaum) the variance is a Volterra process,

\[ v_t = v_0 + rac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^t (t - s)^{\alpha - 1} igl(\lambda( heta - v_s)\,ds + u\sqrt{v_s}\,dB_s igr), \qquad \alpha = H + frac12, \]

and the characteristic function of \(X_T = \log(S_T/F_T)\) stays semi-closed:

\[ E\,e^{iuX_T} = \exp\Bigl( heta\lambda\int_0^T h(u, s)\,ds + v_0\,I^{1-\alpha}h(u, T)\Bigr), \qquad D^\alpha h = - frac12(u^2 + iu) + (iu ho u - \lambda)h + frac12 u^2h^2, \]

with \(h(u, 0) = 0\). fractional_riccati solves the fractional Riccati equation with the fractional Adams predictor–corrector, vectorised over \(u\). At \(H = 1/2\) the model is Heston with \(\kappa = \lambda\) and \(\xi = u\), and the characteristic function converges to Heston's at second order in the step. RoughHeston prices vanillas by a Fourier integral on the normalised Lewis contour. The explicit predictor becomes unstable at large \(|u|\) when \(H\) is small, so the integral is truncated at \(U = 20/\sqrt{ ar vT}\), beyond which the integrand is negligible. \(E[v_t]\) has a closed form through the Mittag-Leffler function. For \(v_0 = heta = 0.04\), \(\lambda = u = 0.3\), \( ho = -0.7\) and \(H = 0.1\), the one-year implied volatilities at strikes \(0.8\), \(1\) and \(1.2\) (unit forward) are \(23.23\%\), \(17.38\%\) and \(13.63\%\). Between expiries of \(0.0025\) and \(0.01\) years (about one and four days), the log-log slope of the at-the-money skew is within \(0.05\) of \(H - 1/2 = -0.4\).

docs.title: 10.2 Lifted Heston
docs.text: The fractional kernel is a completely monotone function, so it is a mixture of exponentials, \(t^{\alpha-1}/\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^\infty e^{-xt}\,\mu(dx)\). The lifted Heston model of Abi Jaber replaces \(\mu\) by \(n\) atoms \(c_i\delta_{x_i}\) on a geometric grid (lifted_weights). The variance is then a sum of \(n\) Markovian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-like factors, and the Riccati equation becomes a system of \(n\) ordinary equations. LiftedHeston solves it by exponential time differencing. With one factor at speed zero it is classical Heston. As \(n\) grows the smile converges to rough Heston's: in the example of §10.1 the largest one-year gap over strikes \(0.8\)–\(1.2\) is \(1.34\), \(0.79\), \(0.46\) and \(0.24\) vol points for \(n = 5\), \(10\), \(20\) and \(50\). Lifted Heston is Markovian in a finite state, so it can be simulated and fed to PDE solvers, at the cost of a factor count that grows as maturities get shorter.

docs.title: 10.3 Calibration
docs.text: calibrate_rough_heston fits \((v_0, \theta, \nu, \rho, H)\) to implied-volatility smiles by bounded least squares, with \(\lambda\) fixed by default because it is weakly identified alongside \(\theta\). Fitted to its own smiles at three expiries from \(0.1\) to \(1.5\) years, it recovers the parameters to a relative \(10^{-8}\). That needs enough Adams steps (n_steps, 400 by default) for the explicit scheme to stay stable up to \(U\). With 100 steps at \(H = 0.08\), a third to a half of the Fourier nodes diverge and are dropped. The values just before them are inaccurate, so the model vols are not smooth enough in the parameters for a finite-difference Jacobian. Where the fit then stalls depends on floating-point rounding, and so on the platform. Fixing \(H = 1/2\) (classical Heston) on the same smiles leaves an RMSE above one vol point: no choice of \(\nu\) and \(\rho\) makes the skew steep at \(0.1\) years and still right at \(1.5\) years.

docs.title: 10.4 Rough Bergomi
docs.text:
Rough Bergomi (Bayer, Friz & Gatheral) models the forward variance curve \(\xi_t(u) = E_t[v_u]\) directly:

\[ v_t = \xi_0(t)\exp\Bigl(\eta\widetilde W_t - \tfrac12\eta^2\operatorname{Var}\widetilde W_t\Bigr), \qquad \widetilde W_t = \sqrt{2H}\int_0^t (t - s)^{H - 1/2}\,dW_s, \]

with spot driven by \(\rho\,dW + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,dW^\perp\). It fits any initial term structure \(\xi_0\) by construction, but it has no characteristic function. rbergomi_paths uses the hybrid scheme of Bennedsen, Lunde & Pakkanen. The kernel's singular first cell is sampled exactly, jointly with \(dW\), and the rest of the convolution uses the optimal discretisation points through an FFT. The compensator uses the scheme's own variance, so \(E[v_t] = \xi_0(t)\) holds on the grid. On the same grid, the smile agrees with exact Cholesky simulation of the Volterra process (spxa.rough.RoughBergomi). Prices use the mixed estimator of Romano & Touzi: conditional on \(W\), \(\log S_T\) is Gaussian, so the orthogonal noise integrates out in a Black formula. At \(\rho = -0.9\) only \(19\%\) of the variance is orthogonal, and the standard error falls by a factor of about \(1.3\) at the money and \(1.7\) at strike \(1.2\).

calibrate_rbergomi fits \((H, \eta, \rho, \xi_0)\) to one smile with common random numbers. Every evaluation reuses one fixed sample, so the objective is a smooth deterministic function and a finite-difference least-squares solver applies. Quotes generated from the same sample are fitted exactly. Quotes from an independent simulation with ten times as many paths, fitted with \(\eta\) and \(\rho\) free and \(H\) at its true value, leave an RMSE of \(0.3\) vol points. That residual is the Monte Carlo error of the calibration sample, and it moves \((\eta, \rho)\) from \((1.6, -0.85)\) to \((1.56, -0.86)\).

docs.title: 10.5 VIX
docs.text:
The squared VIX index at \(T\) is the 30-day forward variance, \(\mathrm{VIX}_T^2 = \frac1\Delta\int_T^{T+\Delta}\xi_T(u)\,du\) with \(\Delta = 30/365\) (VIX_WINDOW). In rough Bergomi, \(\xi_T(u) = \xi_0(u)\exp(\eta G_u - \frac12\eta^2\operatorname{Var}G_u)\), where \(G_u = \sqrt{2H}\int_0^T(u - s)^{H-1/2}\,dW_s\) is Gaussian. Its covariance has a closed form through \({}_2F_1\). RBergomiVIX puts the window on 24 Gauss–Legendre nodes and samples \(\mathrm{VIX}_T^2\) exactly, so the only error is Monte Carlo noise. A moment-matched lognormal gives a fast approximation. For \(H = 0.1\), \(\eta = 1.9\) and \(\xi_0(t) = 0.04 + 0.01t\) at \(T = 0.5\):

  • \(\sqrt{E[\mathrm{VIX}_T^2]} = 21.31\%\);
  • the futures price is \(18.04\%\) (lognormal approximation: \(17.98\%\)), the gap being Jensen's concavity adjustment;
  • VIX option implied volatilities rise only from \(81.2\%\) to \(81.9\%\) between strikes \(0.14\) and \(0.36\);
  • at-the-money VIX implied volatility falls with expiry: \(135.5\%\), \(97.6\%\), \(66.5\%\) and \(53.6\%\) at \(0.05\), \(0.25\), \(1\) and \(2\) years.

Lognormal forward variances make the VIX nearly lognormal, so the VIX smile is almost flat, while the market's slopes clearly upward.

In Heston, \(E_T[v_u]\) is affine in \(v_T\), so \(\mathrm{VIX}_T^2 = av_T + b\) with \(a = (1 - e^{-\kappa\Delta})/(\kappa\Delta)\) and \(b = \theta(1 - a)\). HestonVIX integrates against the noncentral \(\chi^2\) law of \(v_T\). The substitution \(x = y^p\) removes the density's singularity at zero when the Feller condition fails, and a smile takes a few milliseconds. For \((v_0, \kappa, \theta, \xi, \rho) = (0.04, 1.5, 0.04, 0.5, -0.7)\) at \(T = 0.5\), the futures price is \(17.06\%\) against \(\sqrt{E[\mathrm{VIX}_T^2]} = 20\%\). The VIX smile slopes down, from \(94.8\%\) at strike \(0.12\) to \(76.0\%\) at \(0.30\), the wrong sign against the market.

docs.title: 10.6 Joint SPX/VIX calibration
docs.text: calibrate_heston_joint fits Heston to SPX smiles (SmileQuote), VIX futures and VIX option smiles (VIXQuote) together, with a weight per block. With consistent quotes it recovers the parameters. The interesting case is the market's: take SPX smiles and VIX futures from one Heston model, and give the VIX options an upward skew of \(+0.4\) per unit of log-moneyness. An SPX-only fit is exact on SPX and on the futures, but misses the VIX smile by \(17\) vol points RMS. The joint fit cuts that to \(3.6\) vol points, at the cost of \(2.0\) vol points on SPX and \(2.0\) VIX points on the futures. It does this by raising the vol of variance to \(\xi = 1.66\), far beyond the Feller condition, so that mass piles up near zero variance. This is the SPX/VIX joint calibration problem: models that price SPX options well disagree with VIX options. It is a standard argument for rough and path-dependent volatility models.

docs.title: 11.1 Marginals and the convex order
docs.text: A smile at one expiry fixes the law of \(X = S_T/F_T\) (§5). For two expiries \(T_1 < T_2\), the laws \(\mu\) of \(X\) and \(\nu\) of \(Y = S_{T_2}/F_{T_2}\) are all that vanillas reveal about the joint law of \((X, Y)\). Absence of arbitrage adds one constraint: \((X, Y)\) is a martingale, \(E[Y \mid X] = X\). Strassen's theorem says a martingale coupling exists if and only if \(\mu \le_{cx} \nu\), that is, the means are equal and every call is worth at least as much at \(T_2\) as at \(T_1\). This is the calendar condition of §1. marginal_from_calls builds the law on an even strike grid whose call function is the linear interpolant of the quotes. Its weights are second differences of the prices. Truncating the grid loses the tails, and an exponential tilt \(p_i e^{\beta k_i}\) restores the unit mean exactly. Rounding-level calendar violations are repaired by flooring the later calls with the earlier ones: a maximum of convex functions is convex. surface_marginals does this for a whole surface. The grid must cover the tails. On the SSVI surface of §8, a grid that stops at \(k = 0.2\) loses the put value below it (\(4.76 \times 10^{-5}\) at one year).

docs.title: 11.2 Bounds by linear programming
docs.text:
The model-free price interval of a claim \(c(X, Y)\) is the minimum and maximum of \(E_\pi[c]\) over martingale couplings \(\pi \in \mathcal M(\mu, \nu)\). On grids this is a linear programme. mot_solve solves it with HiGHS. Its dual is the cheapest superhedge,

\[ \varphi(x) + \psi(y) + h(x)(y - x) \ge c(x, y), \]

with no duality gap (Beiglböck, Henry-Labordère & Penkner): vanillas \(\varphi\) on \(T_1\) and \(\psi\) on \(T_2\), plus \(h(X)\) units of the forward from \(T_1\) to \(T_2\). For a forward-start straddle \(|Y - X|\) between flat 20% smiles at \(0.5\) and \(1\) year, mot_bounds gives \([0.0507, 0.1389]\), which contains the Black–Scholes value \(0.1127\). Dropping the martingale constraint, classical optimal transport (ot_solve) gives the much wider \([0.0466, 0.2721]\). A claim \(\varphi(X) + \psi(Y) + g(X)(Y - X)\) is replicated by vanillas and the forward, so its interval has zero width. The same holds for \((Y - X)^2\) and the forward log contract \(\log Y - \log X\). HiGHS presolve has to be switched off, because tail weights of \(10^{-14}\) make it report infeasibility.

docs.title: 11.3 Entropic transport
docs.text: Penalising the plan with \(\varepsilon\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \mu\otimes\nu)\) gives a Gibbs-form solution, \(\pi_{ij} \propto \mu_i\nu_j\exp\bigl((c_{ij} - a_i - b_j - h_i(y_j - x_i))/\varepsilon\bigr)\). mot_sinkhorn finds the potentials by alternating closed-form log-sum-exp updates for \(a\) and \(b\) with Newton steps on each row's martingale condition for \(h\), and decreases \(\varepsilon\) geometrically with warm starts. Each iteration costs \(O(nm)\) and needs no LP solver. The plans are feasible, so their values approach the LP bounds from inside. For the straddle above, the gap to the upper bound is \(3.0 \times 10^{-3}\) at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-2}\) and \(2.0 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(\varepsilon = 3 \times 10^{-3}\).

docs.title: 11.4 Hedges as trades, and a backtest
docs.text: The dual potentials live on the grid. static_replication writes any grid-piecewise-linear function as cash, a forward and a strip of calls whose weights are the slope changes. The superhedge then becomes concrete trades: calls on \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) costing exactly the upper bound, plus \(h(X)\) forwards entered at \(T_1\) for free. robust_bounds runs the whole chain from a surface for forward-start payoffs (forward_start_call, forward_start_straddle). superhedge_pnl evaluates hedge minus payoff along simulated paths, interpolating the potentials linearly between nodes. Take Heston marginals (\(v_0 = \theta = 0.04\), \(\kappa = 1.5\), \(\xi = 0.5\), \(\rho = -0.7\)) at \(0.5\) and \(1\) year on a 121-node grid, and a forward-start at-the-money call. The bounds are \([0.0205, 0.0606]\), and the Heston price on 50,000 paths is \(0.0457\). Along those paths the superhedge never loses more than \(0.0009\), under 4% of the grid spacing, an interpolation error between nodes. Its mean gain equals the gap between the bound and the model price. Paths must stay on the grid: on a coarser grid ending at \(0.2\), the hedge has no instruments below the last strike and loses on paths that fall there.

docs.title: 11.5 Several dates
docs.text: mot_multi bounds claims \(c(X_1, \dots, X_n)\) over joint laws that are martingales in their own filtration, with one constraint per path prefix. A claim on two consecutive dates has the same bounds as the two-marginal problem, because any coupling extends by a Markov kernel. Intermediate smiles can only tighten a claim on the first and last dates. With flat 20% smiles at \(0.5\), \(1\) and \(1.5\) years, a three-date Asian call on the average of \(X_1, X_2, X_3\), struck at the forward, lies in \([0.0634, 0.0778]\), around the Black–Scholes value \(0.0705\).

docs.title: 12.1 Replication
docs.text:
A variance swap pays the realised variance \(\frac1T\int_0^T v_t\,dt\) against a fixed strike. For a continuous price process, Itô's formula applied to \(\log S\) turns the integrated variance into a static position in the log contract plus a dynamic forward hedge. Carr–Madan then writes the log contract as a strip of out-of-the-money options with weight \(1/K^2\). In log moneyness \(k = \log(K/F_T)\) and with undiscounted prices \(\mathrm{OTM}(k)\) over the forward, the fair strike is

\[ K_{\text{var}}\,T = 2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{OTM}(k)\, e^{-k}\,dk . \]

The gamma swap weights realised variance by \(S_t/S_0\), and its strike uses the weight \(1/K\), which drops the factor \(e^{-k}\). fair_variance integrates a vectorised OTM pricer by composite Gauss–Legendre quadrature on panels scaled by the at-the-money total volatility. variance_swap_strike and gamma_swap_strike apply it to a surface. A flat smile returns \(\sigma^2\) to \(10^{-12}\). Replication on Fourier prices recovers Heston's \(E[V]/T\) to \(10^{-6}\) and rough Heston's \(\frac1T\int_0^T E[v_t]\,dt\) to \(2 \times 10^{-5}\). With negative skew, the \(1/K^2\) weight loads the expensive puts. On the SSVI surface of §8 at one year, \(K_{\text{var}} = 0.0569\), above the gamma swap strike \(0.0494\), which is above the at-the-money variance \(0.043\). variance_swap_mtm values a seasoned swap from realised and remaining fair variance.

docs.title: 12.2 Term structure and the VIX
docs.text: The strikes \(K_i\) at expiries \(T_i\) fix the integrated forward variance \(\int_0^{T_i}\xi_0 = K_i T_i\). ForwardVarianceCurve interpolates it with \(\xi_0\) flat between expiries and rejects strikes whose total variance falls. It is the input of the forward-variance models in §10. Built from the SSVI surface and passed to rough Bergomi, it reproduces the 30-day strike as \(E[\mathrm{VIX}_0^2]\) exactly and the one-year strike as the mean of \(\int_0^1 v_t\,dt\) over simulated paths. The VIX index itself is the 30-day replication, \(100\sqrt{K_{\text{var}}(30/365)}\). vix_index gives \(21.61\) on the SSVI surface.

docs.title: 12.3 Volatility swaps
docs.text:
A volatility swap pays \(\sqrt{V/T}\). Concavity puts its strike below \(\sqrt{K_{\text{var}}}\), and the gap depends on the dynamics, not only on the smile. In Heston the Laplace transform of \(V = \int_0^T v_t\,dt\) is exponential-affine (the CIR bond-price formula), and

\[ E\sqrt V = \frac{1}{2\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{1 - E e^{-sV}}{s^{3/2}}\,ds . \]

heston_volatility_swap evaluates this after substituting \(s = u^2\). It writes the transform with \(g - \kappa = 2\xi^2 s/(g + \kappa)\), so it stays accurate as \(\xi \to 0\), where the strike tends to \(\sqrt{E[V]/T}\). For \(v_0 = 0.04\), \(\kappa = 1.5\), \(\theta = 0.06\), \(\xi = 0.5\) and \(\rho = -0.7\), the one-year volatility swap is \(0.2090\) against \(\sqrt{K_{\text{var}}} = 0.2228\), and an Euler simulation of \(V\) agrees within its standard error.

docs.title: 12.4 Discrete monitoring
docs.text: Term sheets use daily log returns, \(\sigma_R^2 = \frac1T\sum_i(\log S_{t_i}/S_{t_{i-1}})^2\), often capped at \(2.5^2 K\). realised_variance and variance_swap_payoff compute these. Under Black–Scholes with step \(\Delta t\), the drift of the log return adds a bias, \(E[\sigma_R^2] = \sigma^2 + \sigma^4\Delta t/4\). The demeaned convention with divisor \(n - 1\) removes it. On daily Heston paths the bias is below the Monte Carlo error, and realised variance prices the swap at \(E[V]/T\).

docs.title: 13.1 Coherent and penalised measures
docs.text:
Models calibrated to the same smiles agree on vanillas but not on path-dependent claims. Cont (2006) measures the disagreement over a set of models \(\mathcal Q\), each with calibration error \(\epsilon_Q\):

\[ \mu_\delta(X) = \sup_{\epsilon_Q \le \delta} E_Q[X] - \inf_{\epsilon_Q \le \delta} E_Q[X]. \]

It is coherent in \(X\): subadditive and positively homogeneous, zero on claims every model prices alike, and unchanged by adding them. Charging each model for its error instead of using a hard tolerance gives the convex version, with upper price \(\max_Q(E_Q[X] - \lambda\epsilon_Q)\) and lower price \(\min_Q(E_Q[X] + \lambda\epsilon_Q)\). Its width falls monotonically in \(\lambda\) to the spread among the best-fitting models. ModelRisk implements both, for exact or Monte Carlo prices. significant tests a width against the simulation error. smile_rmse is the usual calibration error. Every martingale model with the given marginals lies inside the MOT interval of §11, and share gives the fraction of that interval a family spans.

docs.title: 13.2 Mixing fractions
docs.text: Calibrate local volatility (\(\eta = 0\)) and SLV with \(\eta = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 1\) (§9) to the SSVI surface of §8. All three fit the smiles at \(0.5\) and \(1\) year within 15 bp, and their vanilla prices agree to calibration noise. Forward-start calls \((Y - kX)^+\) between \(0.5\) and \(1\) year do not agree. Local volatility prices them highest and the full Heston mix lowest, a relative spread of 7% at the money and 21% at \(k = 1.1\). All prices lie inside the MOT bounds, yet the family covers only 2%, 8% and 11% of the bounds at \(k = 0.9, 1, 1.1\). The space of models that fit the smiles is far larger than one SLV family. On the SLV PDE, a one-year up-and-out call (barrier 130, strike 100) moves by 9% across the family and a down-and-out (barrier 85) by 1%. A variance swap is fixed by replication (§12), and all three models price it at \(K_{\text{var}}\). The one-year volatility swap spreads by \(0.008\), falling as the vol of variance rises with \(\eta\).

docs.title: 14.1 Stress testing
docs.text:
surface_price values the EuropeanOption contracts of spxa.risk on a surface stored in the market dictionary under <id>_SURFACE, so StressTestingEngine scenarios reach the smile. A spot move scales every forward by \(S/S_0\). Against a base market, the change in <id>_VOL is a parallel vol shift and the change in r multiplies discount factors by \(e^{-\Delta r T}\) and forwards by \(e^{\Delta r T}\). Under sticky strike the vol is read at the strike, \(\sigma(K, T)\). Under sticky moneyness it is read at the shifted log-moneyness \(\log(K/F)\), so the smile moves with the forward. Moving the forward to \(F + h\) then gives the delta of §7.2, \(\Delta_{BS} - \mathcal V_{BS}\,\sigma_k/F\), and a put's delta is less negative on a downward skew.

A parallel shift of continuously compounded zero rates is exactly \(P \mapsto Pe^{-\Delta r T}\), \(F \mapsto Fe^{\Delta r T}\). So under sticky moneyness a rate scenario on a surface over a bootstrapped OIS curve reprices to \(10^{-12}\) like rebuilding the surface on the shifted curve.

docs.title: 14.2 Surfaces of zoo processes
docs.text: process_vol_surface (and Process.to_vol_surface) turns an exponential-Lévy model \(S_T = S_0e^{(r-q)T + X_T}\) from spxa.zoo into a surface. It prices out-of-the-money options by Lewis's formula, inverts Black at strikes spaced in at-the-money standard deviations, and fits raw SVI per expiry. The model vols are exact: for a Merton jump diffusion they match the Poisson series to \(10^{-8}\). Take \(\sigma = 15\%\), half a jump a year of mean \(-10\%\) and spread \(15\%\), with \(r = 3\%\), \(q = 1\%\) and expiries from 3 months to 2 years. The surface then shows a downside skew that flattens with maturity, and SVI misses the model smile by 12.4 bp at most.

docs.title: 14.3 Graph nodes
docs.text:
spxa.graph.vol gives the SVI total variance as a node of its five parameters, with the analytic gradient

\[ \partial_b w = \rho(k - m) + R,\quad \partial_\rho w = b(k - m),\quad \partial_m w = -b\Bigl(\rho + \frac{k - m}{R}\Bigr),\quad \partial_\sigma w = \frac{b\sigma}{R}, \]

where \(R = \sqrt{(k - m)^2 + \sigma^2}\) and \(\partial_a w = 1\). It also gives the value of an option on a surface as a node of spot and a parallel vol shift, whose vector–Jacobian product is the adapter's delta and vega.

docs.title: Tutorial 1 — First Composition¶
docs.text: This notebook introduces the core idea of spxa: stochastic processes as first-class algebraic objects. You write Z = X + c*Y or W = X @ T and get back a new process with exact analytical properties.

docs.title: 1. Adding two processes¶
docs.text: For independent Lévy processes $X$ and $Y$, the sum $Z = X + Y$ has triplet $$ (b_Z, \sigma^2_Z, u_Z) = (b_X + b_Y,\; \sigma^2_X + \sigma^2_Y,\; u_X + u_Y) $$ This is exact — not an approximation.

docs.title: 2. Scalar multiplication¶
docs.text: For $Z = c \cdot X$, the triplet transforms as $$ (b_Z, \sigma^2_Z, \nu_Z) = (cb + \Delta b,\; c^2 \sigma^2,\; \nu(\cdot/c)) $$ The drift correction $\Delta b$ accounts for mass shifting across the unit ball under the truncation function.

docs.title: 3. Cumulant table¶
docs.text: Every EXACT process exposes analytical cumulants via the Lévy–Khintchine formula. The cumulant table also computes skewness and excess kurtosis.

docs.title: 4. Subordination¶
docs.text: Subordinating Brownian motion by a Gamma process gives the Variance Gamma model. The @ operator does this: W = BM @ Gamma.

docs.title: 5. The Story: derivation trace¶
docs.text: .__story__() produces a human-readable derivation of how the current process was constructed.

docs.title: 6. LaTeX rendering (Jupyter only)¶
docs.text: In a Jupyter environment, you can render the derivation as LaTeX:

docs.title: 7. Property lattice¶
docs.text: Properties propagate automatically. The library is honest when they are lost.

docs.title: Tutorial 2 — Finance Models¶
docs.text:
spxa is purpose-built for quantitative finance. This notebook covers:

  • Exponential Lévy models for asset prices
  • European option pricing via the Carr-Madan FFT method
  • Implied volatility smile from VG and NIG models
  • Comparing models via Hellinger and L² distances

docs.title: 1. Geometric Lévy models¶
docs.text: The exponential Lévy model is $S_t = S_0 \exp(rt + X_t)$ where $X$ is a Lévy process. The risk-neutral drift is chosen so $\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0 e^{rt}$.

docs.title: 2. European option pricing — Carr-Madan FFT¶
docs.text: For a Lévy log-return process $X$ with characteristic function $\phi(u;t)$, the call price is given by the Carr-Madan formula: $$ C(K) = \frac{e^{-\alpha k}}{\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-iuk} \psi(u)\, du $$ where $k = \log(K/S_0)$ and $\psi$ is a modified version of $\phi$.

docs.title: 3. Cumulant comparison¶
docs.text: The cumulants directly encode the shape of the distribution — skewness and kurtosis are why Lévy models produce smiles.

docs.title: 4. Model distances¶
docs.text: spxa computes L² and Hellinger distances between marginal distributions directly from the characteristic functions — no Monte Carlo needed.

docs.title: 5. Stochastic volatility via subordination¶
docs.text: The Variance Gamma model is exactly a BM subordinated by a Gamma process. The subordinator acts as a stochastic clock — business time vs calendar time.

docs.title: Tutorial 3 — Physics Applications¶
docs.text:
Lévy processes appear throughout statistical physics:

  • Anomalous diffusion — fractional BM and α-stable processes
  • First passage times — exact Lévy distribution
  • Stochastic volatility via subordination — random time changes
  • Hawkes processes — self-exciting point processes in neuroscience and seismology

docs.title: 1. Anomalous diffusion: fractional Brownian motion¶
docs.text:
Standard BM has $\text{Var}(B_t) = \sigma^2 t$ (linear in $t$). Fractional BM with Hurst index $H$ has $$\text{Var}(B^H_t) = \sigma^2 t^{2H}$$

  • $H = 0.5$: standard diffusion (Brownian)
  • $H > 0.5$: superdiffusion (long memory, persistent increments)
  • $H < 0.5$: subdiffusion (anti-persistent increments)

docs.title: 2. Mean-square displacement¶
docs.text: MSD$(t) = \mathbb{E}[|X_t - X_0|^2]$ is a key observable in single-particle tracking experiments. For fBM: MSD$(t) = 2\sigma^2 t^{2H}$.

docs.title: 3. Heavy-tailed diffusion: α-stable processes¶
docs.text: For $\alpha < 2$, the $\alpha$-stable process has power-law tails: no finite variance, no finite mean for $\alpha \leq 1$. This describes Lévy flights observed in animal foraging, plasma turbulence, and financial returns.

docs.title: 4. First passage times¶
docs.text: The time for BM to hit a level $a > 0$ follows the Lévy distribution: $$P(\tau \leq t) = 2\Phi(-a/(\sigma\sqrt{t}))$$ This is an $\alpha=1/2$ stable distribution — heavy-tailed with infinite mean.

docs.title: 5. Hawkes process — self-exciting events¶
docs.text: The Hawkes process models event clustering: each event increases the probability of future events. Applications: earthquake aftershocks, neural spike trains, high-frequency order book arrivals.

docs.title: 6. OU-Lévy — stochastic volatility¶
docs.text: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process driven by a Gamma subordinator is the Barndorff-Nielsen–Shephard stochastic volatility model. The variance process $V_t$ is stationary, non-negative, and mean-reverting.
